lesson.arabic-weak-verbs.family_en: Hollow verb: the middle root letter is و
steps: The root ق-و-ل is about saying. Its middle letter is و, a weak letter, so it changes shape: a long ā in قَالَ, a long ū in يَقُولُ, and a plain w in the noun قَوْل.
The present puts a prefix in front, and the prefix tells you who: أَقُولُ I say, تَقُولُ you say, يَقُولُ he says, نَقُولُ we say.

Now the forms that look odd: قُلْتُ (I said), قُلْ (say!) and لَمْ يَقُلْ (he didn't say). In all three the ل has no vowel of its own (a sukūn), and in a verb a long vowel doesn't stay right before a letter with a sukūn. So the long vowel shortens to u.
Give the ل a vowel again and the long vowel comes back: قَالُوا (they said), and قُولِي, which is "say!" to a woman.
Before the article al-, two letters without a vowel would meet, so قُلْ takes a helping i: قُلِ الْحَقَّ, tell the truth.

examples.en: He is telling the truth.

words.en: the truth (the -a ending: it's what he says)

examples.en: Tell the truth!

words.en: say! (to a man; the i joins it to the next word)
the truth (the -a ending: it's what is said)

examples.en: What is he saying?

words.en: is he saying (Arabic needs no "is" or "does")

why.q_en: If يَقُولُ already means "he says", why add هُوَ?
why.a_en: You don't have to. The يَـ at the front already means "he", so يَقُولُ on its own is a whole sentence: he says. Add هُوَ when you want to stress who is speaking, often in contrast with someone else. Compare يَقُولُ الْحَقَّ, he tells the truth, with هُوَ يَقُولُ الْحَقَّ, he (not someone else) tells the truth.

selftest.q_en: How do you tell a man "Say!"?
selftest.why_en: The ل has a sukūn, so the long ū shortens: قُلْ. يَقُولُ means "he says".

selftest.q_en: What does نَقُولُ mean?
selftest.why_en: The prefix نَـ means "we". "I say" is أَقُولُ, and "you say" is تَقُولُ.

selftest.q_en: Why is there no long ū in لَمْ يَقُلْ?
choices: After لَمْ the ل has a sukūn, so the long ū shortens
It comes from a different root
selftest.answer: After لَمْ the ل has a sukūn, so the long ū shortens
selftest.why_en: After لَمْ the last letter takes a sukūn, as in لَمْ يَكْتُبْ. In a verb, a long vowel doesn't stay before a sukūn, so ū becomes u. The root is still ق-و-ل.

leads_to.en: قَالَ in reporting: قَالَ إِنَّ.

lesson.arabic-weak-verbs.family_en: Hollow verb: the middle root letter is و
steps: The root ك-و-ن has و in the middle, and its present يَكُونُ has a long ū, just like يَقُولُ. So كَانَ / يَكُونُ behaves just like قَالَ / يَقُولُ.
Where the ن has a sukūn, the long vowel shortens to u: كُنْتُ (I was), كُنْ (be!) and لَمْ يَكُنْ (he wasn't).
In the present, Arabic usually leaves "is" out: يُوسُفُ مُعَلِّمٌ means "Yūsuf is a teacher", with no verb at all.
For the past you need كَانَ, and the description after it takes the -a ending: كَانَ يُوسُفُ مُعَلِّمًا, Yūsuf was a teacher.
You need يَكُونُ where Arabic wants a verb: for the future, usually with سَـ in front (سَيَكُونُ, it will be), and after لَمْ or أَنْ.

examples.en: I was at home yesterday.
The weather will be nice tomorrow.

words.en: nice (the -an ending comes from the verb "be")

examples.en: The restaurant wasn't open.

words.en: didn't (it makes the present form past and negative)
be (the i joins it to the next word)
open (the -an ending comes from the verb "be")

why.q_en: If Arabic leaves "is" out, why does يَكُونُ exist?
why.a_en: The present "is" is left out in a plain statement, but you need a verb for the future (سَيَكُونُ, it will be) and after words such as أَنْ that are always followed by a verb: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَكُونَ طَبِيبًا, I want to be a doctor.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I was"?
selftest.why_en: The ن has a sukūn before -tu, so the long vowel shortens to u: كُنْتُ. أَكُونُ means "I am" or "I will be".

selftest.q_en: What does يُوسُفُ مُعَلِّمٌ mean?
selftest.why_en: There is no verb: in the present Arabic leaves "is" out. "Was" needs كَانَ, and "will be" needs سَيَكُونُ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "he wasn't"?
selftest.why_en: لَمْ is followed by the present form, and the ن takes a sukūn, so the long ū shortens: لَمْ يَكُنْ.

leads_to.en: كَانَ's sisters: أَصْبَحَ, لَيْسَ, مَا زَالَ.

lesson.arabic-weak-verbs.family_en: Hollow verb: the middle root letter is ي
steps: The root ع-ي-ش has ي in the middle. It's hollow like قَالَ, but with ي instead of و.
In the present the ي shows as a long ī: يَعِيشُ, أَعِيشُ, تَعِيشُ, نَعِيشُ.
Where the ش has a sukūn, the long vowel shortens, as in قُلْتُ. But here it shortens to i, not u: عِشْتُ (I lived), عِشْ (live!) and لَمْ يَعِشْ (he didn't live).
A handy guide: look at the long vowel of the present. ū gives u: يَقُولُ, قُلْتُ. ī gives i: يَعِيشُ, عِشْتُ.
If the present has a long ā, the short vowel is i: خَافَ / يَخَافُ, be afraid, gives خِفْتُ, I was afraid; نَامَ / يَنَامُ, sleep, gives نِمْتُ, I slept.

examples.en: I live with my family.
Where do you live?
I lived in a small village.

why.q_en: Where has the ي gone in عِشْتُ?
why.a_en: It's still in the root, ع-ي-ش. In عَاشَ it's hidden in the long ā, and in يَعِيشُ it shows as a long ī. In عِشْتُ the ش has a sukūn, so the long vowel shortens, to i, the short form of the ī in يَعِيشُ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I lived"?
selftest.why_en: The present يَعِيشُ has a long ī, so the shortened vowel is i. A long ā can't stay before the sukūn.

selftest.q_en: What does نَعِيشُ mean?
selftest.why_en: The prefix نَـ means "we", and the long ī shows it's the present. "I live" is أَعِيشُ.

selftest.q_en: خَافَ means "he was afraid". Which means "I was afraid"?
selftest.why_en: Its present, يَخَافُ, has a long ā, and ā gives i: خِفْتُ, like نِمْتُ from نَامَ.

lesson.arabic-weak-verbs.family_en: Final-weak verb: the last root letter is و
steps: دَعَا / يَدْعُو means "invite" or "call (someone to come)". Its root is د-ع-و, and the last root letter, و, is weak.
At the end of دَعَا the و is hidden in a long ā, written with an ordinary alif. In the present it shows as a long ū: يَدْعُو, أَدْعُو, تَدْعُو, نَدْعُو.
Add an ending that starts with a consonant, such as -tu (I) or -nā (we), and the و comes back as a w: دَعَوْتُ, I invited; دَعَوْنَا, we invited.
"They invited" is دَعَوْا: the root's vowel and the plural ending merge into -aw. The alif at the end is written but not said, as in قَالُوا.
The noun دَعْوَة, an invitation, shows the و plainly.
For what happens after لَمْ, see مَشَى / يَمْشِي: verbs that end in a long vowel all follow the same rule there.

examples.en: I invited Laylā to dinner.
Yūsuf invites his friends every week.

words.en: his friends (-a: the ones invited; -hu: his)

examples.en: Who did you invite?

why.q_en: Why does دَعَا end in an ordinary alif, when مَشَى ends in ى?
why.a_en: The spelling shows the hidden root letter. دَعَا comes from د-ع-و, so its final ā is written with an ordinary alif. مَشَى comes from م-ش-ي, so its final ā is written ى. Both sound the same.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I invited"?
selftest.why_en: Before -tu the root's و comes back: دَعَوْتُ. A form with y belongs to a verb whose root ends in ي, like مَشَيْتُ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "we invite"?
selftest.why_en: The prefix نَـ means "we" in the present. دَعَوْنَا is "we invited", and أَدْعُو is "I invite".

selftest.q_en: What is the root of يَدْعُو?
selftest.why_en: يَـ is the present prefix, not a root letter, and the long ū at the end shows that the last root letter is و.

lesson.arabic-weak-verbs.family_en: Final-weak verb: the last root letter is ي
steps: The root م-ش-ي ends in ي, so مَشَى / يَمْشِي is final-weak, like دَعَا but with ي.
At the end of مَشَى the ي is hidden in a long ā, written ى. In the present it's a long ī: يَمْشِي, أَمْشِي, تَمْشِي, نَمْشِي.
Before -tu the ي comes back as a y: مَشَيْتُ, I walked; مَشَيْنَا, we walked. "They walked" is مَشَوْا, with the same -aw ending as دَعَوْا.

After لَمْ, a regular verb loses its last vowel: يَكْتُبُ becomes لَمْ يَكْتُبْ. In يَمْشِي the last vowel is the long ī itself, so it shortens to i and the ي is no longer written: لَمْ يَمْشِ, he didn't walk.
The command works the same way: اِمْشِ, walk! (to a man).
رَمَى / يَرْمِي, throw, follows the same pattern: رَمَيْتُ, I threw; لَمْ يَرْمِ, he didn't throw.

examples.en: I walk to work every day.
We walked in the park.
Yūsuf didn't walk today.

words.en: walk (the long ī has shortened to i)

why.q_en: If ي is a root letter, how can لَمْ make it disappear?
why.a_en: In forms like these, لَمْ takes away the last vowel of the present. In يَكْتُبُ that's a short u; in يَمْشِي it's the long ī. A short i stays behind, so you still hear it. The ي is still in the root, م-ش-ي: it just isn't written in this form.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I walked"?
selftest.why_en: Before -tu the root's ي comes back: مَشَيْتُ. A form with w belongs to a verb whose root ends in و, like دَعَوْتُ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "he didn't walk"?
selftest.why_en: لَمْ is followed by the present form, and it takes away the last vowel: the long ī shortens to i, so the ي isn't written.

selftest.q_en: رَمَى / يَرْمِي means "throw". Which means "throw!" to a man?
selftest.why_en: Like اِمْشِ, the command shortens the long ī to i. اِرْمِي is what you say to a woman, and رَمَى means "he threw".

lesson.arabic-irregular-families.family_en: Initial-weak verb: the first root letter is و

table.en: a stop (for buses or taxis); a position

steps: The root of وَقَفَ / يَقِفُ is و-ق-ف: the و is the first root letter.
In the past the و is there in every form: وَقَفَ, وَقَفْتُ, وَقَفُوا.
In the present it drops out, and the vowel after the first remaining letter is i: يَقِفُ, أَقِفُ, تَقِفُ, نَقِفُ.
The command is made from the present, so it has no و either: قِفْ, stop! Just two letters. You'll see it on road signs.
Nouns keep the و: مَوْقِف is a stop for buses or taxis, or a position on something.
وَضَعَ / يَضَعُ, put, also drops its و in the present (وَضَعْتُ, I put; يَضَعُ, he puts), though its vowel there is a, not i.

examples.en: Stop here!
The bus stops in front of the station.

words.en: stops (it starts with t- because the bus is feminine)

examples.en: We stood at the stop for an hour.

words.en: for an hour (the -an ending: how long)

why.q_en: If يَقِفُ has no و, how do I find it in a dictionary?
why.a_en: Try a root that starts with و. When a present form has only two root letters left, with a short vowel between them, the missing first letter is often و. So for يَقِفُ, look up و-ق-ف, under وَقَفَ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "he stands"?
selftest.why_en: In the present the first root letter, و, drops out: يَقِفُ.

selftest.q_en: What does قِفْ mean?
selftest.why_en: It's the command, made from the present يَقِفُ without its prefix. "He stopped" is وَقَفَ, and "a stop" is مَوْقِف.

selftest.q_en: You meet يَصِلُ, "he arrives". Which root would you look up?
selftest.why_en: يَـ is the present prefix. Only two root letters are left, with i between them, so try a first و: و-ص-ل, under وَصَلَ.

lesson.arabic-irregular-families.title_en: Reply, give back: رَدَّ and يَرُدُّ
lesson.arabic-irregular-families.family_en: Doubled verb: the last two root letters are the same
steps: رَدَّ / يَرُدُّ means "reply" (رَدَّ عَلَى, reply to) or "give back". Its root, ر-د-د, ends in the same letter twice.
When the two د come together, Arabic writes them once, with a shadda: رَدَّ, رَدُّوا, يَرُدُّ.
Add -tu (I) or -nā (we) and the last د has a sukūn. A shadda can't work then, so the two letters are written out: رَدَدْتُ, I replied; رَدَدْنَا, we replied.
In the present the vowel u comes before the shadda: يَرُدُّ, أَرُدُّ, تَرُدُّ, نَرُدُّ.
The command is usually رُدَّ. You may also see the longer اُرْدُدْ: its last د has a sukūn, so the pair is written out, just as in رَدَدْتُ.
مَرَّ / يَمُرُّ, pass by, works the same way: مَرَرْتُ, I passed; يَمُرُّ, he passes.

examples.en: Laylā replied to my message.
I'll give the book back tomorrow.

words.en: the book (the -a ending: what is given back)

examples.en: When did they reply?

why.q_en: Why does رَدَدْتُ have two د, when رَدَّ has only one?
why.a_en: رَدَّ has two as well: the shadda means "this letter twice". A shadda works only when a vowel follows it, as in رَدَّ. Before -tu the last د has a sukūn instead, so the two letters are written out in full: رَدَدْتُ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "we replied"?
selftest.why_en: Before -nā the last د has a sukūn, so the pair is written out: رَدَدْنَا. رَدَّتْ is "she replied", and نَرُدُّ is "we reply".

selftest.q_en: What does يَرُدُّ mean?
selftest.why_en: The prefix يَـ and the u before the shadda show the present. "He replied" is رَدَّ, and "reply!" is رُدَّ.

selftest.q_en: مَرَّ means "he passed". Which means "I passed"?
selftest.why_en: As in رَدَدْتُ: before -tu the last root letter has a sukūn, so the doubled letter is written out twice.

lesson.arabic-irregular-families.family_en: Hamzated verb: the first root letter is a hamza
steps: The root of أَخَذَ / يَأْخُذُ is أ-خ-ذ. Its first letter is a hamza, a full consonant: the catch in the throat before a vowel.
Most forms are regular, and the hamza simply stays: أَخَذْتُ, أَخَذُوا, يَأْخُذُ, نَأْخُذُ.
Watch "I take". The prefix for "I" is أَـ, and the root starts with a hamza too. Two hamzas in a row join into one long ā, written آ: آخُذُ.
The command is the real surprise: خُذْ, take! The hamza drops out completely.
Two other common verbs do the same: أَكَلَ, eat, gives كُلْ, and أَمَرَ, order (give an order), gives مُرْ. Most other hamza verbs keep their hamza in the command, as in اِسْأَلْ, ask!

examples.en: Take the key!

words.en: take! (to a man; the i joins it to the next word)
the key (the -a ending: what is taken)

examples.en: Who took my pen?

examples.ar: آخُذُ كِتَابًا مِنَ الْمَكْتَبَةِ كُلَّ أُسْبُوعٍ.
examples.en: I take a book out of the library every week.

words.en: a book (the -an ending: what is taken)
from (the a joins it to the next word)

why.q_en: Why does "I take" begin with آ?
why.a_en: "I" in the present starts with أَ, and this root starts with a hamza as well. Two hamzas side by side are hard to say, so the second becomes a long ā, and the pair is written as one letter with a madda: آخُذُ. You'll see the same in آكُلُ, I eat.

selftest.q_en: How do you tell a man "Take!"?
selftest.why_en: أَخَذَ is one of the few verbs whose command drops the hamza: خُذْ. يَأْخُذُ means "he takes".

selftest.q_en: Which means "I take"?
selftest.why_en: The prefix أَـ plus the root's hamza gives آ. أَخَذْتُ is "I took", and نَأْخُذُ is "we take".

selftest.q_en: أَكَلَ means "he ate". Which means "eat!" to a man?
selftest.why_en: Like خُذْ, the command of أَكَلَ drops the hamza: كُلْ. يَأْكُلُ is "he eats", and أَكَلْتُ is "I ate".

lesson.arabic-irregular-families.family_en: Hamzated verb: the middle root letter is a hamza
steps: The root of سَأَلَ / يَسْأَلُ is س-أ-ل: the hamza is the middle letter. Unlike أَخَذَ, nothing drops out, and every form keeps all three root letters.
What changes is how the hamza is written. Inside a word it usually sits on a seat: an alif (أ), a wāw (ؤ) or a yāʾ without dots (ئ).

The seat follows the vowels: look at the hamza's own vowel and the vowel before it. If either is i, the seat is ئ. Otherwise, if either is u, it's ؤ. Otherwise it's usually أ. After a long ā it sits on the line instead: قِرَاءَة, reading.
So سَأَلَ and يَسْأَلُ have a and no vowel around the hamza: أ. سُؤَال, a question, has u before it: ؤ. أَسْئِلَة, questions, has i on it: ئ.
The usual command keeps the hamza and starts with اِ: اِسْأَلْ, ask! You may also meet a short form, سَلْ.

examples.en: I asked Laylā the way.

words.en: about (the i joins it to the next word)

examples.en: Ask the teacher!

words.en: ask! (to a man; the i joins it to the next word)
the teacher (the -a ending: the one asked)

examples.en: This is a hard question.

why.q_en: Why is the hamza written three different ways in one family?
why.a_en: It's always the same sound, a catch in the throat. Only its seat changes, to suit the vowels next to it: i gives ئ, u gives ؤ, and a usually gives أ. When you look a word up, treat all three as the same root letter.

selftest.q_en: Which is the right spelling of "a question"?
selftest.why_en: The vowel before the hamza is u, and there's no i, so the seat is ؤ.

selftest.q_en: Which means "ask!" to a man?
selftest.why_en: The command starts with اِ and ends in a sukūn. سَأَلَ is "he asked", and يَسْأَلُ is "he asks".

selftest.q_en: In أَسْئِلَة, questions, why does the hamza sit on ئ?
choices: It's near the end of the word
selftest.why_en: An i on the hamza or just before it always gives the seat ئ.

lesson.arabic-derived-forms.title_en: One root, three verbs: عَلِمَ, عَلَّمَ and تَعَلَّمَ
lesson.arabic-derived-forms.family_en: Derived forms: form I, form II and form V of one root
steps: Arabic builds new verbs from one root by fitting it into fixed patterns. The root ع-ل-م is about knowing, and three of its verbs are very common.
Form I is the plain root: عَلِمَ, he knew (or found out); يَعْلَمُ, he knows.
Form II doubles the middle root letter: عَلَّمَ, he taught, that is, he made someone know. Form II often has this "make someone …" meaning, but not always, so check each new verb.
Form V puts تَـ in front of form II: تَعَلَّمَ, he learned. Pairs like this are common (غَيَّرَ, he changed something; تَغَيَّرَ, it changed), but treat the pattern as a clue, not a rule.
Listen to the first vowel of the present: form II has yu- (يُعَلِّمُ), while forms I and V have ya- (يَعْلَمُ, يَتَعَلَّمُ).

The doer's noun swaps the present's prefix for مُـ and has i before the last letter: يُعَلِّمُ, he teaches, gives مُعَلِّم, a teacher; يَتَعَلَّمُ, he learns, gives مُتَعَلِّم, a learner. تَعْلِيم is the action of form II: teaching, education.

examples.en: Do you know where the station is?

words.en: (turns the sentence into a yes-or-no question)

examples.en: Yūsuf teaches at a school nearby.
I'm learning to swim this summer.

why.q_en: Why does يُعَلِّمُ start with yu-, when يَتَعَلَّمُ starts with ya-?
why.a_en: It depends on the form, not the meaning. Forms II, III and IV have u in the prefix: يُعَلِّمُ, يُسَاعِدُ (he helps), يُرْسِلُ (he sends). Form I and forms V to X have a: يَعْلَمُ, يَتَعَلَّمُ, يَسْتَخْدِمُ (he uses). So the first vowel is a clue to the form.

selftest.q_en: Which means "he teaches"?
selftest.why_en: Form II: the doubled ل and yu- at the front. يَتَعَلَّمُ is "he learns", and يَعْلَمُ is "he knows".

selftest.q_en: What does مُتَعَلِّم mean?
selftest.why_en: مُـ with form V gives the one who learns. A teacher is مُعَلِّم, and knowledge is عِلْم.

selftest.q_en: قَدَّمَ, he presented, is form II. Which means "he presents"?
selftest.why_en: Form II's present starts with yu- and keeps the doubled letter: يُقَدِّمُ. يَتَقَدَّمُ is form V (he moves forward), and يَقْدَمُ is form I (he arrives).

lesson.arabic-verb-moods.title_en: Three endings for one present verb: يَكْتُبُ, لَنْ يَكْتُبَ, لَمْ يَكْتُبْ
lesson.arabic-verb-moods.family_en: The moods of the present verb: what each ending is called, and the small words that call for it

table.en: until he writes, so that he writes

steps: A present verb, a مُضَارِع, changes its last vowel with the small word before it. On its own it ends in -u: يَكْتُبُ. Grammar calls this مَرْفُوع, the indicative.
After أَنْ, لَنْ, حَتَّى and لِكَيْ, it ends in -a: لَنْ يَكْتُبَ, he won't write. This is مَنْصُوب, the subjunctive.
After لَمْ, and after لَا meaning "don't", it ends in a sukūn: لَمْ يَكْتُبْ, he didn't write. This is مَجْزُوم, the jussive.
The small word decides the ending, so learn each with its ending: لَمْ and a sukūn, لَنْ and -a.
These are the endings of a regular verb like يَكْتُبُ. Some verbs show the change in other ways (the next explainer).

examples.en: I want to write a letter.
I'll stay here until Salmā comes back.
Sāmī didn't write the assignment.

why.q_en: Why does لَا تَكْتُبْ end in a sukūn, when لَا يَكْتُبُ keeps -u?
why.a_en: They're two different words لَا. The one meaning "not" leaves the verb as it is: لَا يَكْتُبُ, he doesn't write. The one meaning "don't" tells someone not to, and the verb after it is مَجْزُوم: لَا تَكْتُبْ, don't write. The ending shows which one you're reading.

selftest.q_en: Which ending does a present verb take after لَنْ?
selftest.why_en: لَنْ, like أَنْ and حَتَّى, calls for the subjunctive, مَنْصُوب.

selftest.q_en: Which is "he didn't write"?
selftest.why_en: After لَمْ the verb is مَجْزُوم, with a sukūn. لَا with -u is "he doesn't write".

selftest.q_en: In لَا تَكْتُبْ, what does لَا mean?
selftest.why_en: The sukūn shows it: after لَا meaning "not", the verb would keep -u.

leads_to.en: إِنْ, if, with the jussive: إِنْ تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ.
لِكَيْ, so that, with the -a ending: لِكَيْ أَصِلَ.

lesson.arabic-verb-moods.title_en: When the mood isn't a vowel: لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا, لَا تَنْسَ
lesson.arabic-verb-moods.family_en: How the five verbs and verbs with a long vowel show the subjunctive and the jussive

table.form_en: a long vowel at the end, after لَا, "don't"
a long vowel inside, after لَمْ

steps: Five present forms end in نَ after a long vowel: يَكْتُبُونَ, they write; تَكْتُبُونَ, you all write; تَكْتُبِينَ, you write (to a woman); يَكْتُبَانِ and تَكْتُبَانِ, the two of them, the two of you. Grammar calls them the five verbs.
They show the mood with that نَ, not with a vowel: plain, it stays; after لَنْ, لَمْ, أَنْ and لَا meaning "don't", it goes.
When ـُونَ loses its نَ, an alif is written after the wāw and not said, as in the past كَتَبُوا: لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا.

A verb with a long vowel shortens it in the jussive. At the end, the long vowel's letter goes: تَنْسَى, you forget, becomes لَا تَنْسَ, don't forget. Inside, the vowel gets short before the sukūn: يَقُولُ becomes لَمْ يَقُلْ, as يَكُونُ becomes لَمْ يَكُنْ.

examples.en: They didn't come to the meeting yesterday.

words.en: come, attend: no نَ after لَمْ

examples.en: You should rest a little (to a woman).

examples.ar: يَا سَلْمَى، لَا تَنْسَيْ مَوْعِدَ الطَّبِيبِ.
examples.en: Salmā, don't forget the doctor's appointment.

why.q_en: لَنْ يَكْتُبُوا and لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا look the same. How do you tell them apart?
why.a_en: By the small word before them. For the five verbs, the subjunctive and the jussive both drop the نَ, so the verb alone can't show "won't" or "didn't": لَنْ looks ahead, لَمْ looks back.

selftest.q_en: Which is "they didn't write"?
selftest.why_en: After لَمْ the نَ goes and an alif is written after the wāw. With no wāw, it's "he didn't write".

selftest.q_en: To a woman, which is "you won't be late"?
selftest.why_en: تَتَأَخَّرِينَ is one of the five verbs: after لَنْ its نَ goes, and nothing is added.

selftest.q_en: Which is "he didn't say"?
selftest.why_en: Before the sukūn, the long ū of يَقُولُ gets short.

lesson.arabic-passive-voice.title_en: The passive: فَتَحَ and فُتِحَ, يَفْتَحُ and يُفْتَحُ
lesson.arabic-passive-voice.family_en: How vowels make a verb passive, in the past and the present
steps: The passive says what was done, not who did it, and Arabic makes it by changing the verb's vowels.
In the past it has u on the first letter and i before the last: فَتَحَ, he opened, becomes فُتِحَ, it was opened.
In the present it has u on the prefix and a before the last letter: يَفْتَحُ, he opens, becomes يُفْتَحُ, it is opened.

Derived forms work the same way: أَرْسَلَ, he sent, becomes أُرْسِلَ, it was sent. In the present the prefix already has u, so only the vowel before the last letter changes: يُرْسِلُ, he sends, becomes يُرْسَلُ, it is sent.
The endings for who stay as in the active: فُتِحَتْ, it (feminine) was opened; وُلِدْتُ, I was born.

examples.en: The museum was opened to visitors.
It is said that the restaurant is excellent.
The letter was sent in the morning.

words.en: was sent (-i before the next word)

why.q_en: Why is it قِيلَ, with a long ī, when فُتِحَ has u then i?
why.a_en: قَالَ is a hollow verb: its middle letter is a long vowel. In the passive the u and i run together into a long ī: قِيلَ, it was said; بِيعَ, it was sold. The present follows يُفْتَحُ, with a long ā: يُقَالُ, it is said.

selftest.q_en: What is the passive of سَمِعَ, he heard?
selftest.why_en: u on the first letter, i before the last: "it was heard".

selftest.q_en: Which is "it is sent"?
selftest.why_en: The a before the last letter makes it passive. With i it's "he sends"; the past passive is "it was sent".

selftest.q_en: What does يُقَالُ mean?
selftest.why_en: The present passive of قَالَ, with u on the prefix and a long ā.

lesson.arabic-passive-voice.title_en: Who did it? نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ, and a doer left unnamed
lesson.arabic-passive-voice.family_en: What the passive does to a sentence: the object takes the doer's place, and the doer goes unnamed

table.form_en: active: the doer, then the object
passive: the object in the doer's place

table.en: the doer's deputy: the passive subject

steps: In an active sentence the doer, the فَاعِل, ends in -u, and the object in -a: سَرَقَ اللِّصُّ الْحَقِيبَةَ, the thief stole the bag.
In the passive the doer goes, and the object takes its place and its -u: سُرِقَتِ الْحَقِيبَةُ, the bag was stolen. Grammar calls it نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ, the doer's deputy.
The verb agrees with it as with a doer: سُرِقَتْ, with -at, because حَقِيبَة is feminine.
The passive is for when the doer is unknown, obvious or beside the point, as often in the news. Read only what it says: سُرِقَتِ الْحَقِيبَةُ doesn't say who stole it, so don't add a doer.
Grammar calls a passive verb الْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْمَجْهُولِ, built for the unknown, and an active one الْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْمَعْلُومِ, built for the known.

examples.en: Sāmī's car was stolen at night.

words.en: the car (of): -u, in the doer's place

examples.ar: أُغْلِقَ الطَّرِيقُ صَبَاحًا، وَلَمْ يُذْكَرِ السَّبَبُ.
examples.en: The road was closed in the morning, and no reason was given.

words.en: was given, was mentioned (-i before the next word)

examples.en: Laylā was born in a small town.

why.q_en: If the passive leaves out the doer, how do you say who did it?
why.a_en: Use the active: سَرَقَ اللِّصُّ الْحَقِيبَةَ, the thief stole the bag. Some formal writing, especially in the news, adds مِنْ قِبَلِ, by, after a passive verb. It's common, but style guides prefer the active: when you know the doer, the active is clearer.

selftest.q_en: Which is "the car was stolen"?
selftest.why_en: Passive vowels, -at for a feminine noun, and the car with -u in the doer's place. With a then a, it would mean the car stole.

selftest.q_en: In the passive, which ending does the noun in the doer's place take?
selftest.why_en: It's نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ, so it ends in -u like a doer.

selftest.q_en: What does مَجْهُول mean in الْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْمَجْهُولِ?
selftest.why_en: A passive verb is "built for the unknown": its doer isn't named.

leads_to.en: In the news, the passive leaves a source unnamed: أُعْلِنَ, it was announced.

lesson.arabic-relative-clauses.title_en: Who, which, that: الَّذِي and its family
lesson.arabic-relative-clauses.family_en: Relative words: they link a noun to the sentence that describes it

table.form_en: one man, or a masculine thing
one woman, a feminine thing, or things in the plural
men, or a mixed group (people only)

steps: Arabic links a noun to a sentence that describes it with a relative word, much like "who", "which" or "that". الَّذِي is for one man or a masculine thing, الَّتِي for one woman or a feminine thing.
The relative word matches the noun: الطَّالِبُ الَّذِي, the student (a man) who; الطَّالِبَةُ الَّتِي, the student (a woman) who; الطُّلَّابُ الَّذِينَ, the students who.
Things in the plural count as feminine singular, so they take الَّتِي: الْكُتُبُ الَّتِي, the books that.

After a noun, a relative word is used only when the noun is definite: one with الْـ, a name, or a possessive. After a noun without الْـ, the describing sentence follows directly, with no relative word.
When the noun is the one the action is done to, the describing sentence points back to it with a pronoun: الْمَدِينَةُ الَّتِي زُرْتُهَا, the city that I visited (literally "that I visited it").
When the noun is the one doing the action, the verb already points back, so no extra pronoun is needed: الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي يَسْكُنُ هُنَا, the man who lives here.
For two, use اللَّذَانِ and اللَّتَانِ. After a preposition, or as an object, they become اللَّذَيْنِ and اللَّتَيْنِ.

examples.en: The shirt I bought is blue.

words.en: I bought it (-hu points back to the shirt)

examples.en: I read a story that I liked a lot.

words.en: a story (no الْـ, so no relative word)

examples.en: I thanked the neighbours who helped us.

words.en: the neighbours (the -a ending: the ones thanked)

why.q_en: Why does a plural like الْكُتُبُ take الَّتِي, not الَّذِينَ?
why.a_en: الَّذِينَ is only for people. Plurals of things are treated as feminine singular: you say الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ, the books are new, with a feminine singular describing word, and in the same way الْكُتُبُ الَّتِي, the books that.

selftest.q_en: "The girl who studies with me": which word links الْبِنْتُ to تَدْرُسُ مَعِي?
selftest.why_en: الْبِنْتُ is one girl, so الَّتِي. الَّذِي is for one man.

selftest.q_en: "The friends who visited us": which relative word goes with الْأَصْدِقَاءُ?
selftest.why_en: Friends are people, and there are several of them, so الَّذِينَ. الَّتِي would suit things in the plural.

selftest.q_en: Which of these takes الَّتِي?
selftest.why_en: Things in the plural take الَّتِي. Men take الَّذِينَ, and one house takes الَّذِي.

lesson.arabic-inna-kana.title_en: إِنَّ and its sisters: إِنَّ, أَنَّ, لَكِنَّ, لَعَلَّ
lesson.arabic-inna-kana.family_en: Particles that make the noun after them end in -a

table.en: I know that the weather is nice
it's as if we were in summer

steps: A sentence such as الْجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ has a subject and a description, and both end in -u (the description with tanween: -un).
Put إِنَّ in front and the subject changes to -a, while the description keeps its -u: إِنَّ الْجَوَّ جَمِيلٌ.
Its sisters work the same way and add their own meaning: أَنَّ, that; لَكِنَّ, but; لَعَلَّ, perhaps (hoping); كَأَنَّ, as if.
إِنَّ starts a statement, or follows قَالَ. أَنَّ follows another word, usually a verb such as أَعْرِفُ, I know.
A pronoun can join straight on: إِنَّهُ, أَنَّهَا, لَعَلَّكَ. With "I" and "we" you'll see both إِنِّي and إِنَّنِي, and both are correct.
Don't confuse أَنَّ with أَنْ. أَنْ comes before a verb (أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنَامَ, I want to sleep), and أَنَّ before a noun or a pronoun.

examples.en: I heard that the museum is closed today.
Perhaps the train will arrive soon.
The house is small, but it's comfortable.

why.q_en: Do I always translate إِنَّ as "indeed"?
why.a_en: No. إِنَّ gives a statement weight, a little like "indeed" or "truly", but English usually leaves it out: إِنَّ الْعِلْمَ نُورٌ is simply "knowledge is light". After قَالَ it means "that": قَالَتْ إِنَّهَا مَشْغُولَةٌ, she said that she was busy.

selftest.q_en: Which is right?
selftest.why_en: After إِنَّ the subject ends in -a (الطَّقْسَ), and the description keeps its -un (بَارِدٌ).

selftest.q_en: Which says "I know that the shop is closed"?
selftest.why_en: After a verb like أَعْرِفُ, use أَنَّ, and the noun after it ends in -a. أَنْ goes before a verb.

selftest.q_en: What does لَعَلَّ add to a sentence?
selftest.why_en: لَعَلَّ is "perhaps", often with hope. "As if" is كَأَنَّ, and "but" is لَكِنَّ.

leads_to.en: إِنَّ after قَالَ, and أَنَّ after other reporting verbs.

lesson.arabic-inna-kana.title_en: كَانَ and its sisters: كَانَ, أَصْبَحَ, لَيْسَ, مَا زَالَ
lesson.arabic-inna-kana.family_en: Verbs that make the description after them end in -a
steps: كَانَ and its sisters are verbs that work on a whole sentence like الْجَوُّ بَارِدٌ. The subject keeps its -u, and the description changes to -a (here -an): كَانَ الْجَوُّ بَارِدًا.
That's the opposite of إِنَّ, which changes the subject and leaves the description alone.
Each adds its own meaning: كَانَ, was; أَصْبَحَ, became; لَيْسَ, is not; مَا زَالَ, still is.
Like any verb, they change for the subject: كَانَتِ الْغُرْفَةُ بَارِدَةً, the room was cold; أَصْبَحْتُ مُعَلِّمًا, I became a teacher.

مَا زَالَ looks negative and past (literally "hasn't stopped"), but it means "still", about now: مَا زَالَ الْجَوُّ بَارِدًا, the weather is still cold. The present-tense form لَا يَزَالُ means the same: لَا يَزَالُ الْمَطَرُ غَزِيرًا, the rain is still heavy.

examples.en: The journey was long.

words.en: was (-at: the journey is feminine; the i joins it to the next word)

examples.en: Yūsuf became a doctor.
The restaurant isn't far.

why.q_en: Why is لَيْسَ in this family, when it means "is not"?
why.a_en: Because it works exactly like كَانَ: its subject keeps -u and its description takes -a, as in لَيْسَ الْمَطْعَمُ بَعِيدًا. It's a verb too, and changes for the person (لَسْتُ مُتْعَبًا, I'm not tired), though it has only this one tense: there is no present or future لَيْسَ.

selftest.q_en: Which of these changes the description, not the subject?
selftest.why_en: كَانَ and its sisters change the description to -a. إِنَّ and لَعَلَّ change the subject.

selftest.q_en: Which says "the room was clean"?
selftest.why_en: After كَانَ the description takes -an (نَظِيفَةً) and the subject keeps -u. كَانَتْ also agrees with the feminine الْغُرْفَةُ.

selftest.q_en: What does مَا زَالَ الْمَطَرُ غَزِيرًا mean?
choices: The rain is no longer heavy
selftest.why_en: مَا زَالَ means "still", though it looks negative.

lesson.arabic-reported-information.title_en: Saying who said it: قَالَ إِنَّ and ذَكَرَ أَنَّ
lesson.arabic-reported-information.family_en: Reporting verbs, and the "that" after them
steps: When you report what someone said, a reporting verb and "that" keep their words apart from your own.
After قَالَ, "that" is إِنَّ, with i. After almost every other reporting verb it's أَنَّ, with a: ذَكَرَ أَنَّ, أَكَّدَ أَنَّ.
Both work like إِنَّ: the noun after them ends in -a, or a pronoun joins on. قَالَتْ إِنَّ الدَّرْسَ مُفِيدٌ; ذَكَرَ أَنَّهُ مَشْغُولٌ.
Change the person to fit the report. Laylā says أَنَا مَشْغُولَةٌ, "I'm busy", and you report قَالَتْ إِنَّهَا مَشْغُولَةٌ, she said she was busy.
The verb shows how sure the speaker is: أَكَّدَ presents it as certain, ظَنَّ as a guess, and زَعَمَ hints that the writer doubts it. Reporting a claim doesn't make it true.
Arabic keeps the speaker's own tense. Where English shifts "is" to "was", Arabic leaves مَشْغُولَةٌ as it was said.

examples.ar: ذَكَرَتْ سَلْمَى أَنَّ الْحَفْلَةَ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ.
examples.en: Salmā mentioned that the party is on Thursday.
Yūsuf said he would be a little late.
The seller claimed that the price was fair.

why.q_en: Does قَالَتْ إِنَّهَا مَشْغُولَةٌ mean that she is busy, or that she was?
why.a_en: It can be either. Arabic keeps the speaker's tense, so مَشْغُولَةٌ doesn't change; English usually shifts it to "was". The context tells you whether it's still true.

selftest.q_en: Which word for "that" follows قَالَ?
selftest.why_en: قَالَ is followed by إِنَّ. Most other reporting verbs take أَنَّ, and أَنْ goes before a verb.

selftest.q_en: Which verb hints that the writer doubts the claim?
selftest.why_en: زَعَمَ, "claimed", often hints at doubt. أَكَّدَ presents a claim as certain, and أَوْضَحَ as an explanation.

selftest.q_en: What does ظَنَنْتُ أَنَّكَ مَشْغُولٌ suggest?
choices: I supposed you were busy, and may have been wrong
Someone told me you were busy
selftest.answer: I supposed you were busy, and may have been wrong
selftest.why_en: ظَنَّ is a supposition. For certainty you'd use أَكَّدَ, and "I was told" is قِيلَ لِي.

lesson.arabic-conditionals.title_en: If and when: إِذَا and إِنْ
steps: A condition sentence has two halves: the condition ("if …") and the result. إِذَا is the everyday "if" or "when", for something you expect, or that may well happen.
After إِذَا, use a past verb, even about the future: إِذَا وَصَلْتَ, if (or when) you arrive. Here the past form doesn't mean it has already happened.
The result starts with فَـ when it begins with سَـ (will), a command or a noun: إِذَا وَصَلْتَ، فَاتَّصِلْ بِي, when you arrive, call me.
إِنْ is a more formal "if". Both its verbs are often in the jussive, the form used after لَمْ: إِنْ تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ, if you study, you'll succeed.
Don't confuse إِنْ, if, with إِنَّ, which gives weight to a statement: the shadda makes the difference.
إِلَّا إِذَا means "unless": سَنَمْشِي إِلَّا إِذَا أَمْطَرَتْ, we'll walk unless it rains.

examples.en: If I finish early, I'll visit you.

words.en: I finish (a past form, about the future)
then I'll visit you (فَـ before سَـ)

examples.ar: إِنْ تُسَافِرْ غَدًا تَجِدِ الطَّرِيقَ مُزْدَحِمًا.
examples.en: If you travel tomorrow, you'll find the road busy.

words.en: you'll find (jussive; the i joins it to the next word)

examples.en: We'll walk unless it rains.

why.q_en: Why is إِذَا followed by a past verb when it's about the future?
why.a_en: That's how Arabic sets up a condition: the past form says "once this happens", and the result says what follows. إِذَا وَصَلْتَ is "if (or when) you arrive", not "if you arrived".

selftest.q_en: Which verb form usually follows إِذَا?
selftest.why_en: إِذَا is usually followed by a past verb, even when the condition is about the future.

selftest.q_en: In إِذَا جَاءَتْ سَلْمَى، نَذْهَبُ مَعًا, which part is the result?
selftest.why_en: The condition is إِذَا جَاءَتْ سَلْمَى, "if Salmā comes". The result is what follows it: نَذْهَبُ مَعًا, we'll go together.

selftest.q_en: What's the difference between إِنْ and إِنَّ?
choices: إِنْ is "if"; إِنَّ gives a statement weight
إِنَّ is "if"; إِنْ gives a statement weight
selftest.answer: إِنْ is "if"; إِنَّ gives a statement weight
selftest.why_en: The shadda makes the difference. إِنْ, if, is often followed by jussive verbs; إِنَّ is followed by a noun ending in -a.

lesson.arabic-conditionals.family_en: Conditions that aren't real, or didn't happen

table.en: if I have time, I'll visit you
if I had time, I'd visit you
if I had known, I'd have told you
if you'd gone with us, you wouldn't have regretted it

table.form_en: if it weren't for, with لَوْلَا
table.en: if it weren't for your help, I'd have been late

steps: لَوْ is for a condition you imagine, usually one that isn't true or didn't happen: لَوْ كَانَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ, if I had time (but I don't).
Its result usually starts with لَـ: لَزُرْتُكَ, I would visit you.
Both halves usually use the past form, even about now or the future. With لَوْ, the past form means "not real" rather than "earlier".
For a result that says what wouldn't happen, use لَمَا: لَمَا نَدِمْتَ, you wouldn't have regretted it.
لَوْلَا means "if it weren't for", and it's followed by a noun in -u: لَوْلَا الْمَطَرُ لَخَرَجْنَا, if it weren't for the rain, we'd have gone out.
Compare إِذَا: إِذَا كَانَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ treats having time as a real possibility, while لَوْ كَانَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ only imagines it.

examples.en: If I were you, I'd accept the offer.
If it weren't for the traffic, we'd have arrived on time.
If I'd known your number, I'd have written to you.

why.q_en: Why do both halves of a لَوْ sentence use the past, even about now?
why.a_en: With لَوْ the past form signals "not real" rather than "earlier". لَوْ كَانَ عِنْدِي وَقْتٌ لَزُرْتُكَ is about now: if I had time (I don't), I'd visit you. The context tells you whether it's about now or about the past.

selftest.q_en: Which sentence imagines something that isn't true?
selftest.why_en: لَوْ imagines it: the weather isn't warm. إِذَا treats it as a real possibility, and the last simply says it's warm.

selftest.q_en: What does لَوْلَا mean?
selftest.why_en: لَوْلَا is "if it weren't for", followed by a noun. "Unless" is إِلَّا إِذَا.

selftest.q_en: How does the result of a لَوْ sentence usually start?
selftest.why_en: The result of لَوْ usually starts with لَـ, as in لَزُرْتُكَ. فَـ is for the result of إِذَا, before سَـ, a command or a noun.

lesson.arabic-cause-purpose-contrast.title_en: Why and what for: لِأَنَّ, بِسَبَبِ, لِكَيْ, لِذَلِكَ
lesson.arabic-cause-purpose-contrast.family_en: Words for reasons, purposes and results
steps: First decide what you mean: a reason (why it happened), a purpose (what it's for) or a result (what followed). Then choose the word.

For a reason, use لِأَنَّ before a sentence and بِسَبَبِ before a noun: تَأَخَّرْتُ لِأَنَّ الطَّرِيقَ مُزْدَحِمٌ, I was late because the road is busy; تَأَخَّرْتُ بِسَبَبِ الزِّحَامِ, I was late because of the traffic.
After لِأَنَّ the noun ends in -a, as after أَنَّ, or a pronoun joins on: لِأَنَّهُ, because he; لِأَنَّنِي, because I.
For a purpose, use لِكَيْ before a verb, which then ends in -a: لِكَيْ أَصِلَ, so that I arrive. مِنْ أَجْلِ goes before a noun: مِنْ أَجْلِ أُسْرَتِي, for my family.
For a result, لِذَلِكَ starts the next part: كَانَ الْمَحَلُّ مُغْلَقًا، لِذَلِكَ رَجَعْتُ, the shop was closed, so I went back.

examples.ar: بَقِيتُ فِي الْبَيْتِ لِأَنَّنِي كُنْتُ مَرِيضًا.
examples.en: I stayed at home because I was ill.

examples.ar: أَتَدَرَّبُ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ لِكَيْ أُشَارِكَ فِي السِّبَاقِ.
examples.en: I train every day so that I can take part in the race.
The road was closed because of the snow.

why.q_en: What's the difference between لِأَنَّ and بِسَبَبِ?
why.a_en: Both give a reason. لِأَنَّ comes before a whole sentence (لِأَنَّ الطَّرِيقَ مُزْدَحِمٌ), and بِسَبَبِ before a noun (بِسَبَبِ الزِّحَامِ). Purpose works the same way: لِكَيْ before a verb, مِنْ أَجْلِ before a noun.

selftest.q_en: Which word introduces a purpose?
selftest.why_en: لِكَيْ, "in order to", names what you're aiming for. لِأَنَّ and بِسَبَبِ give a reason.

selftest.q_en: Which says "I was late because of the rain"?
selftest.why_en: Before a noun, use بِسَبَبِ, and the noun ends in -i. لِأَنَّ needs a whole sentence after it, and لِكَيْ a verb.

selftest.q_en: After لِكَيْ, how does the verb end?
selftest.why_en: After لِكَيْ the verb takes the subjunctive, which ends in -a, as in لِكَيْ أَصِلَ.

lesson.arabic-cause-purpose-contrast.title_en: But, although, whereas: لَكِنَّ, مَعَ أَنَّ, رَغْمَ, بَيْنَمَا

table.form_en: but, before a noun or pronoun
but, before a verb (the light form)

steps: A contrast sets two things against each other. لَكِنَّ, "but", works like إِنَّ: a noun after it ends in -a, or a pronoun joins on, as in لَكِنَّهُ.
Before a verb, use the light form لَكِنْ, without the shadda: أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَحْضُرَ، لَكِنْ تَأَخَّرَ الْقِطَارُ, I wanted to come, but the train was late.
مَعَ أَنَّ, "although", goes before a sentence, and its noun ends in -a, as after أَنَّ: خَرَجْنَا مَعَ أَنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ, we went out although it was cold.
رَغْمَ, "despite", goes before a noun in -i: ذَهَبْنَا رَغْمَ الْمَطَرِ, we went despite the rain. You'll also see بِالرَّغْمِ مِنْ.
بَيْنَمَا sets two things side by side, "whereas" or "while": أَخِي يُحِبُّ الشِّتَاءَ، بَيْنَمَا أُحِبُّ الصَّيْفَ, my brother loves winter, whereas I love summer.
أَمَّا means "as for". The comment after its topic starts with فَـ: أَمَّا أَنَا فَأُفَضِّلُ الشَّايَ, as for me, I prefer tea.

examples.ar: الْفُنْدُقُ غَالٍ، لَكِنَّهُ قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْبَحْرِ.
examples.en: The hotel is expensive, but it's close to the sea.

words.en: to (the a joins it to the next word)

examples.en: Salmā passed despite the difficult exam.
As for Yūsuf, he prefers coffee.

why.q_en: What's the difference between لَكِنَّ and لَكِنْ?
why.a_en: Both mean "but". لَكِنَّ, with a shadda, is followed by a noun or a pronoun, which takes -a: لَكِنَّ الْجَوَّ بَارِدٌ; لَكِنَّهُ. لَكِنْ, the light form, is followed by a verb or a whole sentence: لَكِنْ تَأَخَّرَ الْقِطَارُ.

selftest.q_en: Which is followed by a noun ending in -i?
selftest.why_en: رَغْمَ is followed by a noun in -i (رَغْمَ الْمَطَرِ). After مَعَ أَنَّ and لَكِنَّ the noun ends in -a.

selftest.q_en: Which says "although the weather was cold"?
selftest.why_en: مَعَ أَنَّ goes before a sentence. رَغْمَ needs a noun (رَغْمَ الْبَرْدِ, despite the cold), and لِأَنَّ gives a reason, not a contrast.

selftest.q_en: In أَمَّا أَنَا فَأُفَضِّلُ الشَّايَ, why is there a فَـ?
choices: After أَمَّا and its topic, the comment starts with فَـ
selftest.answer: After أَمَّا and its topic, the comment starts with فَـ
selftest.why_en: أَمَّا, "as for", is answered by فَـ: as for me, (then) I prefer tea.

phrases_ar: أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَحْضُرَ، لَكِنْ تَأَخَّرَ الْقِطَارُ
أَخِي يُحِبُّ الشِّتَاءَ، بَيْنَمَا أُحِبُّ الصَّيْفَ

lesson.arabic-greetings-address.title_en: Talking to a man or a woman: أَنْتَ and أَنْتِ
lesson.arabic-greetings-address.family_en: "You" and "your" change for a man or a woman
steps: When you talk to one person, Arabic has two words for "you": أَنْتَ to a man and أَنْتِ to a woman. Only the last vowel differs: -ta or -ti.
"Your" works the same way, as an ending on the word: -ka to a man, -ki to a woman. اِسْمُكَ is "your name" to a man, and اِسْمُكِ to a woman.
So the question changes with the person you ask: كَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟ to a man, كَيْفَ حَالُكِ؟ to a woman.
Without vowel marks the two look alike, so the last vowel is what you listen for.
أَنَا, "I", is the same word for a man or a woman, and so is بِخَيْرٍ: أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ, I'm well, doesn't change. Some other words about yourself do: طَالِب for a man, طَالِبَة for a woman.

examples.en: My name's Laylā, and what's yours? (to a man)
How are you, Salmā?
You're a student, and you're a teacher.

why.q_en: Why does Arabic need two words for "you"?
why.a_en: Arabic shows whether you're talking to a man or a woman, in "you", in "your" and in many verbs. It isn't about politeness: both forms are equally polite.

selftest.q_en: You're asking a woman how she is. What do you say?
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "your" is -ki: حَالُكِ. -ka is for a man, and حَالِي is "my state".

selftest.q_en: Which word means "you" when you speak to a man?
selftest.why_en: أَنْتَ, with -ta, is for a man; أَنْتِ, with -ti, for a woman. أَنَا is "I".

selftest.q_en: Does أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ change when a woman says it?
choices: No, it's the same for a man or a woman
selftest.answer: No, it's the same for a man or a woman
selftest.why_en: Neither أَنَا nor بِخَيْرٍ changes for a man or a woman, so the whole phrase stays the same.

leads_to.en: Verbs split for a man or a woman too: تَكْتُبُ, تَكْتُبِينَ.

lesson.arabic-greetings-address.family_en: Each greeting has its own answer
steps: Arabic greetings come in pairs: each one has its own reply, so learn them together.
Many replies answer with something brighter: صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ, "morning of good", is answered with صَبَاحُ النُّورِ, "morning of light".
السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ works anywhere, with anyone. The reply turns the words round and adds وَ, "and": وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ.
عَلَيْكُمْ is plural, but it's used for one person too.
When someone thanks you with شُكْرًا, the answer is عَفْوًا, you're welcome.

examples.en: Good morning, Laylā.
Welcome to our home. (to a woman)
Thank you, goodbye.

why.q_en: Why isn't صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ answered with the same words?
why.a_en: It's the custom: the reply matches the greeting and goes one better, "light" for "good". Saying صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ back wouldn't be wrong, but صَبَاحُ النُّورِ is what people expect.

selftest.q_en: Someone says مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ. What's the usual reply?
selftest.why_en: مَسَاءُ is evening, so the reply is مَسَاءُ النُّورِ. صَبَاحُ النُّورِ is for the morning, and مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ means goodbye.

selftest.q_en: What's the reply to السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ?
selftest.why_en: The reply turns the words round and adds وَ: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ.

selftest.q_en: Someone says شُكْرًا to you. What do you answer?
selftest.why_en: عَفْوًا is "you're welcome". It's also "excuse me" or "sorry".

leads_to.en: After hello: short words that keep a conversation going.

lesson.arabic-nominal-sentences.title_en: Saying what something is, with no "is"
lesson.arabic-nominal-sentences.family_en: A sentence without a verb: what you're talking about, and what you say about it

table.form_en: a phrase, not yet a sentence

steps: In the present, Arabic doesn't need a word for "is" or "are": أَنَا طَالِبٌ is "I (am) a student".
A sentence like this has two parts: what you're talking about, and what you say about it.
With الْـ on the first word and none on the second, it's a sentence: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ, the house is big.
With الْـ on both, it's a phrase, not yet a sentence: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ, the big house. Add something to make it one: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ جَدِيدٌ.
For a woman, or a feminine word, the second part usually ends in ة: هِيَ طَبِيبَةٌ; الْغُرْفَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ.

examples.en: I'm an engineer and she's a doctor.
The room is small.

words.en: (is) small (with ة: the room is feminine)

examples.en: The new car is beautiful.

words.en: the new one (with الْـ: part of the phrase)
(is) beautiful (no الْـ: what you say about it)

why.q_en: With no "is", how can I tell a sentence from a phrase?
why.a_en: Look at the second word. If it has الْـ like the first (الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ), it belongs to the name: the big house. If it has no الْـ (الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ), it's what you're saying about the house: the house is big.

selftest.q_en: What does الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ mean?
selftest.why_en: Only the first word has الْـ, so it's a sentence: the book (is) new.

selftest.q_en: Which is a full sentence?
selftest.why_en: الْقَلَمُ صَغِيرٌ is "the pen is small". The other two are phrases: "the small pen" and "a small pen".

selftest.q_en: A man says "I'm busy". Which is it?
selftest.why_en: مَشْغُولَةٌ is what a woman says, and أَنْتَ مَشْغُولٌ is "you're busy".

leads_to.en: كَانَ puts these sentences into the past.

lesson.arabic-simple-questions.title_en: Question words: هَلْ, مَنْ, مَا, أَيْنَ, مَتَى, كَيْفَ
lesson.arabic-simple-questions.family_en: Asking for the piece of information you need
steps: Choose the question word for what you're missing: a person (مَنْ), a thing (مَا), a place (أَيْنَ), a time (مَتَى) or a way (كَيْفَ).
هَلْ at the start turns a statement into a yes/no question: هَلْ أَنْتَ طَالِبٌ؟ The answer is نَعَمْ, yes, or لَا, no.
مَا is "what" before a noun or a pronoun (مَا هَذَا؟), and مَاذَا before a verb (مَاذَا تَدْرُسُ؟).
Before الْـ, هَلْ takes a helping i: هَلِ الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ؟
The question word comes first, and the rest stays as it would in a statement: الْبَيْتُ هُنَا, the house is here; أَيْنَ الْبَيْتُ؟, where is the house?

examples.en: Who's this? This is Salmā.
When is the lesson?
Is the restaurant near?

words.en: (starts a yes/no question; the i joins it to the next word)

why.q_en: Why don't Arabic questions need "is" or "does"?
why.a_en: Just as in statements: أَيْنَ الْبَيْتُ؟ is literally "where the house?", and هَلْ تَدْرُسُ؟ is "do you study?" with no word for "do". The question word does the job.

selftest.q_en: You want to know when the train leaves. Which word do you start with?
selftest.why_en: مَتَى asks about a time. أَيْنَ asks where, and مَنْ who.

selftest.q_en: Which word for "what" goes before a verb?
selftest.why_en: مَاذَا goes before a verb (مَاذَا تَدْرُسُ؟), and مَا before a noun or a pronoun (مَا هَذَا؟).

selftest.q_en: Which is a natural answer to هَلْ أَنْتِ مَشْغُولَةٌ؟
selftest.why_en: A هَلْ question is answered with نَعَمْ or لَا, and you answer about yourself with أَنَا.

leads_to.en: The same question words with past verbs.

lesson.arabic-origin-location.title_en: In, from, to, on: فِي, مِنْ, إِلَى, عَلَى
lesson.arabic-origin-location.family_en: Small words for place, and the -i ending after them

table.en: away from the house; about the house

steps: These small words show where something is, where it comes from or where it's going: فِي, in; مِنْ, from; إِلَى, to; عَلَى, on.
The noun after them ends in -i: فِي الْبَيْتِ, عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ. Without الْـ, it ends in -in: فِي بَيْتٍ, in a house.
Before الْـ, مِنْ becomes مِنَ and عَنْ becomes عَنِ, so the words run on smoothly: مِنَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ, عَنِ الْبَيْتِ.
Where you are and where you're from are different questions: أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ asks where you are now; مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ asks where you're from.
إِلَى is for moving towards a place: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, I go to school. For being in a place, use فِي.

examples.ar: أَنَا مِنْ لُبْنَانَ، وَأَسْكُنُ فِي بِرِيطَانِيَا.
examples.en: I'm from Lebanon, and I live in Britain.

words.en: Lebanon (a name like this takes -a here, not -i, and never -in)

examples.en: The pen is on the table.
The school is near the house.

words.en: from (English just says "near the house"; مِنْ becomes مِنَ before الْـ)

why.q_en: Why does the noun end in -i after فِي?
why.a_en: These little words always put the noun after them in its -i form; it's one of the main jobs of the endings. So the same word can end differently: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ, the house is big, but فِي الْبَيْتِ, in the house.

selftest.q_en: Which ending does a noun take after عَلَى?
selftest.why_en: After فِي, مِنْ, عَلَى and the other small place words, the noun ends in -i: عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ.

selftest.q_en: "I'm going to the market": which word means "to"?
selftest.why_en: إِلَى is for moving towards a place. فِي is "in", and مِنْ is "from".

selftest.q_en: What does مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟ ask?
selftest.why_en: مِنْ أَيْنَ is "from where". "Where are you?" is أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟

leads_to.en: Which small word a verb takes after it.

lesson.arabic-origin-location.title_en: From a place to a describing word: مِصْر, مِصْرِيّ
lesson.arabic-origin-location.family_en: Adding ـِيّ to a place makes "from there"

table.form_en: a man from there (the ـا drops)

steps: To say someone is from a place, add ـِيّ to the place's name: مِصْر, Egypt; مِصْرِيّ, Egyptian.
For a woman, add ـِيَّة instead: مِصْرِيَّة.
If the country's name has الْـ, leave it off: الْعِرَاق, عِرَاقِيّ. If it ends in ـا, drop that too: بِرِيطَانِيَا, بِرِيطَانِيّ.
Use it like any describing word: هُوَ مِصْرِيٌّ وَهِيَ لُبْنَانِيَّةٌ, he's Egyptian and she's Lebanese.
The same ending makes describing words from other nouns too: عَرَبِيّ, Arab or Arabic, from عَرَب, the Arabs.

examples.en: I'm British, and my friend is Iraqi.
Are you Egyptian? (to a woman)
She's from Syria, so she's Syrian.

why.q_en: Why is it عِرَاقِيّ, without الْـ, when the country is الْعِرَاق?
why.a_en: The describing word is made from the name itself, without "the". You add الْـ again only when the phrase needs it, as in الطَّالِبُ الْعِرَاقِيُّ, the Iraqi student.

selftest.q_en: How does a woman from Lebanon describe herself?
selftest.why_en: For a woman, the ending is ـِيَّة. The other two are the word for a man and the name of the country.

selftest.q_en: Which means "Iraqi" for a man?
selftest.why_en: الْعِرَاق is the country, and عِرَاقِيَّة is for a woman.

selftest.q_en: What do you add to a place's name to make "from there", for a man?
selftest.why_en: ـِيّ makes "from there" (ـِيَّة for a woman). ـَة marks the feminine, and ـَات a plural.

leads_to.en: Describing words come after their noun and match it.

lesson.arabic-repair-phrases.title_en: When you don't understand: asking politely
lesson.arabic-repair-phrases.family_en: Phrases that keep a conversation going, to a man or a woman
steps: Not understanding is a normal part of talking in a new language. Say so, and ask for what you need.
Start with عَفْوًا, excuse me, or لَمْ أَفْهَمْ, I didn't understand.
Then ask: أَعِدْ, repeat, and add بِبُطْءٍ, slowly, or مَرَّةً أُخْرَى, once more. Finish with مِنْ فَضْلِكَ, please.
To a woman, the request ends in -ī: أَعِيدِي, and "please" is مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.
For one word you didn't catch, ask about it: مَا مَعْنَى هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَةِ؟

examples.ar: عَفْوًا، أَعِيدِي مَرَّةً أُخْرَى، مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.
examples.en: Excuse me, could you say it again, please? (to a woman)
I didn't understand this word.

words.en: word (the -a ending: what I didn't understand)

examples.en: Speak slowly, please. (to a man)

why.q_en: Isn't it rude to keep asking someone to repeat?
why.a_en: No: asking shows you're listening and want to understand, and it keeps the conversation honest. A polite عَفْوًا at the start and مِنْ فَضْلِكَ at the end is all it takes.

selftest.q_en: How do you ask a woman to repeat?
selftest.why_en: To a woman the request ends in -ī: أَعِيدِي. أَعِدْ is to a man, and أُعِيدُ means "I repeat".

selftest.q_en: What does بِبُطْءٍ add to a request?
selftest.why_en: بِبُطْءٍ is "slowly". "Again" is مَرَّةً أُخْرَى, and "please" is مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.

selftest.q_en: Which question asks what a word means?
selftest.why_en: مَعْنَى is "meaning". The others ask your name and when the lesson is.

leads_to.en: Why it's لَمْ أَفْهَمْ, with a present verb, for "I didn't understand".

lesson.arabic-gender-definiteness.title_en: Masculine and feminine: ة, and the words without it
lesson.arabic-gender-definiteness.family_en: Every noun is masculine or feminine

table.form_en: feminine by meaning, with a ت that isn't ة

steps: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine, things as well as people: قَلَم, pen, is masculine; سَيَّارَة, car, is feminine.
The usual sign of the feminine is ة at the end: طَالِب is a student who's a man, طَالِبَة a student who's a woman.
Some feminine nouns have no ة: some by meaning, like أُمّ, mother; others you simply learn, like شَمْس, sun, and أَرْض, earth.
A word describing a feminine noun takes ة too: الشَّمْسُ كَبِيرَةٌ, the sun is big.
So learn each new noun with its gender, the way you learn its meaning.

examples.en: The mother is a doctor and the father is a teacher.
The sun is hot today.
This is a little girl.

words.en: (is) a girl (feminine by meaning; its ت is part of the word, not ة)

why.q_en: If شَمْس has no ة, how do I know it's feminine?
why.a_en: From the words that go with it: you say الشَّمْسُ كَبِيرَةٌ, with a feminine describing word, and هَذِهِ, not هَذَا. Dictionaries mark it too. That's why it's worth learning a noun's gender along with the noun.

selftest.q_en: Which noun is feminine?
selftest.why_en: سَيَّارَة ends in ة. قَلَم and بَيْت are masculine.

selftest.q_en: Which is right?
selftest.why_en: أَرْض is feminine, even without ة, so its describing word takes ة: كَبِيرَةٌ.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "a teacher" when the teacher is a woman?
selftest.why_en: Add ة: مُعَلِّمَة. مُعَلِّم is a man, and مُعَلِّمَات means several women teachers.

leads_to.en: Describing words take ـَة to match a feminine noun.

lesson.arabic-gender-definiteness.title_en: The article الْـ: sun letters and moon letters

table.form_en: a moon letter: the ل is said
a sun letter: the ل isn't said

steps: الْـ means "the". It's written the same way every time, but it sounds different depending on the letter after it.
Before a moon letter, you hear its ل: الْقَمَر, الْكِتَاب. The ل has a sukūn.
Before a sun letter, the ل isn't said. The next letter is doubled instead, which the shadda shows: الشَّمْس, الدَّرْس.
The sun letters are the ones said with the tip of the tongue: ت, ث, د, ذ, ر, ز, س, ش, ص, ض, ط, ظ, ل, ن. All the others are moon letters.
The spelling doesn't change: the ل stays on the page either way.

examples.en: The sun is in the sky.

words.en: the sun (ش is a sun letter)
the sky (س is a sun letter)

examples.en: The moon is beautiful tonight.

words.en: the moon (ق is a moon letter)
tonight (ل is itself a sun letter)

examples.en: The student is in the library.

words.en: the student (ط is a sun letter)
the library (م is a moon letter)

why.q_en: Why isn't الشَّمْس spelled the way it's said?
why.a_en: The spelling keeps "the" the same in every word, so you can always see it. The shadda on the next letter tells you to skip the ل and double that letter instead.

selftest.q_en: In الدَّرْس, is the ل of الْـ said?
choices: No: د is a sun letter
Yes: د is a moon letter
selftest.answer: No: د is a sun letter
selftest.why_en: د is said with the tip of the tongue, so it's a sun letter: the ل is silent and د is doubled.

selftest.q_en: Which word has a moon letter after الْـ?
selftest.why_en: ب is a moon letter, so the ل is said. س and ن are sun letters.

selftest.q_en: What shows that the ل isn't said?
choices: a shadda on the next letter
selftest.answer: a shadda on the next letter
selftest.why_en: The shadda doubles the sun letter in place of the ل. A sukūn on the ل means it is said.

leads_to.en: الْـ is one of several pieces written joined to a word.
How الْـ joins the word before it when you speak.

lesson.arabic-adjective-agreement.title_en: Describing words: after the noun, and matching it
lesson.arabic-adjective-agreement.family_en: An adjective copies its noun: masculine or feminine, الْـ or not

table.form_en: a sentence (الْـ on the noun only)

steps: A describing word comes after its noun: كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ, a new book (literally "book new").
It copies the noun: feminine if the noun is feminine (سَيَّارَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ), and with الْـ if the noun has الْـ (السَّيَّارَةُ الْجَدِيدَةُ).
If only the noun has الْـ, you've made a sentence: السَّيَّارَةُ جَدِيدَةٌ, the car is new.
You can do both at once: السَّيَّارَةُ الْجَدِيدَةُ سَرِيعَةٌ, the new car is fast.
It copies the ending too: in فِي بَيْتٍ قَدِيمٍ, in an old house, both words end in -in.

examples.en: This is a short story.
The new student is happy.

words.en: the new one (with الْـ: part of the name)
(is) happy (no الْـ: what you say about him)

examples.en: I live in a small flat.

why.q_en: Why does the describing word take الْـ too?
why.a_en: In Arabic a describing word matches its noun in everything: masculine or feminine, الْـ or not, and the ending. الْكِتَابُ الْجَدِيدُ is literally "the book the new". Leaving الْـ off the second word turns it into a sentence: الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ, the book is new.

selftest.q_en: Which means "a big room"?
selftest.why_en: No الْـ on either word: "a big room". الْغُرْفَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ is "the room is big", and الْغُرْفَةُ الْكَبِيرَةُ "the big room".

selftest.q_en: "The long story": which is right?
selftest.why_en: The describing word copies the noun: feminine, with ة, and with الْـ.

selftest.q_en: What does الْوَلَدُ سَعِيدٌ mean?
selftest.why_en: Only الْوَلَدُ has الْـ, so it's a sentence: the boy (is) happy.

leads_to.en: Where a describing word goes after a chain of nouns.

lesson.arabic-plural-basics.title_en: Plurals: added endings, reshaped words, and "she" for things
lesson.arabic-plural-basics.family_en: Two kinds of plural, and how a plural of things is described

table.form_en: men, or a mixed group: add ـُونَ

steps: Some plurals add an ending: ـُونَ for men or a mixed group (مُعَلِّمُونَ), and ـَات for women and for many things (مُعَلِّمَات, سَيَّارَات).
After a preposition, or as the object, ـُونَ becomes ـِينَ: مَعَ الْمُعَلِّمِينَ, with the teachers.
Many plurals reshape the word inside instead: كِتَاب, كُتُب; بَيْت, بُيُوت. You can't work these out, so learn each plural with its singular.
Things in the plural count as "she": هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ, these are books; الْبُيُوتُ قَدِيمَةٌ, the houses are old.
People in the plural take plural words: هُمْ طُلَّابٌ, they're students.

examples.en: The pens are on the desk.
These are new cars.

words.en: new (feminine singular, for a plural of things)

examples.en: The teachers are in the room.

words.en: the teachers (ـُونَ: men, or a mixed group)

why.q_en: Why do things in the plural take "she" words?
why.a_en: That's how Arabic groups them: a plural of things is treated as one feminine whole. So you say هَذِهِ, not هَؤُلَاءِ, and جَدِيدَةٌ, not a plural describing word. هَؤُلَاءِ and plural describing words are for people.

selftest.q_en: What's the plural of بَيْت?
selftest.why_en: بَيْت has a reshaped plural, بُيُوت, which you learn with it.

selftest.q_en: Which says "the pens are new"?
selftest.why_en: Pens are things, so the plural takes the feminine singular: جَدِيدَةٌ. جَدِيدُونَ would be for people.

selftest.q_en: Several teachers, all women: which plural?
selftest.why_en: For women, ة becomes ـَات. مُعَلِّمُونَ and مُعَلِّمِينَ are for men, or a mixed group.

leads_to.en: The form for exactly two, and the plurals made with an ending.

lesson.arabic-demonstratives.title_en: This and that: هَذَا, هَذِهِ, ذَلِكَ, تِلْكَ

table.form_en: this (feminine, or things in the plural)
that (feminine, or things in the plural)

steps: هَذَا and هَذِهِ point to something near: هَذَا for a masculine noun, هَذِهِ for a feminine one.
ذَلِكَ and تِلْكَ point to something further away, in the same way.
For people in the plural, use هَؤُلَاءِ (near) and أُولَئِكَ (far). Things in the plural take هَذِهِ and تِلْكَ, as they take "she" words.
هَذَا بَيْتٌ is a sentence: this is a house. With الْـ, هَذَا الْبَيْتُ is just "this house", and needs more to be a sentence: هَذَا الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ.
هَذَا, هَذِهِ, ذَلِكَ and هَؤُلَاءِ are said with a long ā after the first letter, which isn't written as a letter of its own. أُولَئِكَ has one too, after its ل, and its و is silent.

examples.en: This restaurant is new.
That's an old picture.
These are my friends.

why.q_en: Why is it هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ, not هَؤُلَاءِ, for "these are books"?
why.a_en: هَؤُلَاءِ is only for people. Things in the plural are treated as "she", so they take هَذِهِ: هَذِهِ كُتُبٌ.

selftest.q_en: You point at a car parked far away. Which word do you use?
selftest.why_en: سَيَّارَة is feminine and it's far away, so تِلْكَ. ذَلِكَ is for a masculine noun, and هَذِهِ for something near.

selftest.q_en: Which means "this is a picture"?
selftest.why_en: With no الْـ on صُورَةٌ it's a sentence, and صُورَة is feminine, so هَذِهِ. هَذِهِ الصُّورَةُ is just "this picture".

selftest.q_en: Which word points to several people near you?
selftest.why_en: هَؤُلَاءِ is for several people near you, and أُولَئِكَ for several people further away. هَذِهِ is "this" for one feminine noun, or for things in the plural, not for several people.

lesson.arabic-idafa-possession.title_en: Whose is it? كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ and كِتَابِي
lesson.arabic-idafa-possession.family_en: Two ways to show who something belongs to: joining two nouns, or an ending
steps: To say whose something is, put the owner after the thing: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ is "the book of the student", the student's book.
The first word has no الْـ and no -un ending; the second ends in -i.
For "my", "your", "his" and so on, add an ending to the noun instead: كِتَابِي, my book; كِتَابُكَ, your book.

A word ending in ة says it as t when something follows. If an ending is joined on, it's written ت as well: سَيَّارَتِي, my car. Before a separate word it stays ة on the page: سَيَّارَةُ الْمُعَلِّمِ, the teacher's car.
The pair counts as "the" when the second word has الْـ: بَيْتُ الْمُعَلِّمِ already means "the teacher's house".

examples.en: My neighbour's son is a doctor.
Where's the car key?
Our house is near the sea.

why.q_en: Why doesn't the first word take الْـ?
why.a_en: The second word already makes the pair definite: كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ is "the book of the student", so "the" is there without الْـ on the first word. The pair works as one unit.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "her house"?
selftest.why_en: -hā is "her". -hu is "his", and -ī is "my".

selftest.q_en: "The school's door": which is right?
selftest.why_en: The first word has no الْـ and no -un, and the second ends in -i.

selftest.q_en: In سَيَّارَتِي, why is ة written ت?
choices: Because something is added after it
selftest.answer: Because something is added after it
selftest.why_en: When an ending follows, ة is written ت and said t: سَيَّارَة, سَيَّارَتِي.

leads_to.en: Chains of more than two nouns.

lesson.arabic-present-person.title_en: Present verbs for I, you, he and she: أَكْتُبُ, تَكْتُبُ, يَكْتُبُ
lesson.arabic-present-person.family_en: The letter in front shows who is doing it
steps: A present verb has a letter in front that shows who is doing it: أَـ for "I", تَـ for "you", يَـ for "he".
تَـ is also used for "she", so تَكْتُبُ can be "you write" (to a man) or "she writes". The sentence, or a word like أَنْتَ or هِيَ, makes it clear.
To a woman, "you" also adds ـِينَ at the end: أَنْتِ تَكْتُبِينَ.
The present covers both "I write" and "I'm writing": أَكْتُبُ رِسَالَةً الْآنَ, I'm writing a letter now.
The vowel in the middle isn't always the same, so learn each verb's present with its past: كَتَبَ / يَكْتُبُ, write; عَمِلَ / يَعْمَلُ, work.

examples.en: My father works in an office.
Do you speak Arabic? (to a woman)

words.en: do you speak (تَـ … ـِينَ: to a woman)

examples.en: She goes to university.

why.q_en: If تَكْتُبُ can mean "you write" or "she writes", how do I tell?
why.a_en: From the sentence: who's being spoken to, or about. Said to someone's face, تَكْتُبُ is "you write"; in a story about a woman, it's "she writes". Adding أَنْتَ or هِيَ makes it certain.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I work"?
selftest.why_en: أَـ in front means "I". يَعْمَلُ is "he works", and تَعْمَلُ "you work" or "she works".

selftest.q_en: How do you ask a woman "Do you write in Arabic?"
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "you" is تَـ with ـِينَ at the end: تَكْتُبِينَ.

selftest.q_en: What can تَذْهَبُ mean?
choices: you go (to a man), or she goes
selftest.answer: you go (to a man), or she goes
selftest.why_en: تَـ is used for "you" (to a man) and for "she"; the sentence shows which.

leads_to.en: The same verbs for groups: نَكْتُبُ, يَكْتُبُونَ.

lesson.arabic-present-group.title_en: We, you all and they: نَكْتُبُ, تَكْتُبُونَ, يَكْتُبُونَ
lesson.arabic-present-group.family_en: نَـ for "we", and ـُونَ for more than one person

table.form_en: you all (men, or a mixed group)

steps: نَـ in front means "we": نَكْتُبُ, we write.
For a group, the letter in front is the same as for one person, and ـُونَ goes on the end: تَكْتُبُونَ, you all write; يَكْتُبُونَ, they write.
ـُونَ is for men or a mixed group. For women only, the ending is ـْنَ: هُنَّ يَكْتُبْنَ. You'll mostly just need to recognise it.
You can leave out نَحْنُ, أَنْتُمْ and هُمْ: the verb already says who.

examples.en: We go to the market every week.
What are you all drinking?

words.en: do you drink (تَـ … ـُونَ: you all)

examples.en: The children are playing in the park.

why.q_en: Do I need نَحْنُ in نَحْنُ نَكْتُبُ?
why.a_en: No. نَكْتُبُ already means "we write", because of the نَـ. Add نَحْنُ only to stress "we", perhaps in contrast with someone else.

selftest.q_en: Which means "we work"?
selftest.why_en: نَـ in front means "we". يَعْمَلُونَ is "they work", and تَعْمَلُونَ "you all work".

selftest.q_en: Which means "they go", for a mixed group?
selftest.why_en: يَـ in front with ـُونَ at the end is "they".

selftest.q_en: What does ـُونَ at the end of a verb show?
choices: more than one person: men, or a mixed group
selftest.answer: more than one person: men, or a mixed group
selftest.why_en: ـُونَ marks a group of men or a mixed group. For women only, the ending is ـْنَ.

leads_to.en: Put سَـ in front of these same forms for the future.

lesson.arabic-objects-prepositions.title_en: Who does what to whom: the -a ending, and words like إِلَى
lesson.arabic-objects-prepositions.family_en: What a verb takes after it: a noun straight after, or a small word first
steps: The thing an action is done to comes after the verb (and after the doer, if one is named) and ends in -a: أَقْرَأُ الْكِتَابَ. Without الْـ, it ends in -an: أَقْرَأُ كِتَابًا.
Some verbs take a small word first, and the noun after it ends in -i: أَرْجِعُ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ.
Arabic and English don't always agree on the small word. أَنْتَظِرُ, I wait for, needs none; أَبْحَثُ, I look, takes عَنْ. So learn each verb with what follows it.
One sentence can have both: أَقْرَأُ كِتَابًا فِي الْمَكْتَبَةِ, I read a book in the library.

examples.en: I drink coffee without sugar.
We wait for the bus here.
Yūsuf is looking for work.

why.q_en: Why does كِتَابًا end in -an here, when it's كِتَابٌ elsewhere?
why.a_en: The ending shows the word's job. As the thing being read, it's كِتَابًا. As what you say something is, in هَذَا كِتَابٌ, this is a book, it's كِتَابٌ. After a small word like فِي, it's كِتَابٍ. Same book, different job.

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "I see the house"?
selftest.why_en: What you see comes straight after أَرَى and ends in -a.

selftest.q_en: "I'm waiting for Laylā": which is right?
selftest.why_en: أَنْتَظِرُ takes the person straight after it, with no word for "for".

selftest.q_en: Why is there a عَنْ in أَبْحَثُ عَنْ مِفْتَاحِي?
choices: أَبْحَثُ takes عَنْ for what you're looking for
selftest.answer: أَبْحَثُ takes عَنْ for what you're looking for
selftest.why_en: Each verb has its own way of taking a noun; أَبْحَثُ takes عَنْ. "My" is the -ī ending on مِفْتَاحِي.

leads_to.en: The -u, -a and -i endings, and what each is called.

lesson.arabic-objects-prepositions.title_en: Me, him, her: endings on the verb (أَعْرِفُهُ)
lesson.arabic-objects-prepositions.family_en: "Him", "her" or "it" joined on to the end of a verb
steps: Instead of a separate word for "him" or "her", Arabic adds an ending to the verb: أَعْرِفُهُ, I know him.
They're mostly the endings for "my", "your" and so on: -ka, -ki, -hu, -hā, -nā, -hum. The one that differs is "me": -nī, not -ī: يَعْرِفُنِي.
-hu and -hā also mean "it", for a masculine or a feminine thing: هَذَا قَلَمٌ جَدِيدٌ، أُحِبُّهُ كَثِيرًا, this is a new pen, and I like it a lot.

examples.en: Do you know me?
This is a new bag, and I like it a lot.

words.en: and I like it (-hā: it, the bag)

examples.en: Where's the key? I can't find it.

words.en: I find it (-hu: it, the key)

why.q_en: Why is "me" -nī on a verb, but "my" -ī on a noun?
why.a_en: On a noun, -ī is "my": كِتَابِي, my book. On a verb, an extra n keeps the verb's own ending from blurring into it: يَعْرِفُنِي, he knows me.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I know her"?
selftest.why_en: -hā is "her", and -hu is "him".

selftest.q_en: What does ـنِي mean on the end of a verb?
selftest.why_en: On a verb, ـنِي is "me". "My" is -ī on a noun, and "us" is ـنَا.

selftest.q_en: Which ending means "it" for سَيَّارَة, a feminine word?
selftest.why_en: For a feminine thing, "it" is ـهَا, as for "her". ـهُ is for a masculine thing.

leads_to.en: The same endings on nouns and after small words.

lesson.arabic-preference-existence.title_en: Having, liking, needing: عِنْدِي, أُحِبُّ, أَحْتَاجُ إِلَى
lesson.arabic-preference-existence.family_en: "Have" without a verb, and what follows "like", "need" and "want"
steps: Arabic has no everyday verb for "to have". It says the thing is "at" you: عِنْدِي أَخٌ, I have a brother (literally "at me, a brother").
The ending shows who has it, just as on a noun: عِنْدِي, عِنْدَكَ, عِنْدَهُ, عِنْدَنَا.
The thing you have is the subject of the sentence, so it ends in -un: عِنْدِي سُؤَالٌ, I have a question.
أُحِبُّ takes what you like straight after it, usually with الْـ: أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ. أَحْتَاجُ takes إِلَى: أَحْتَاجُ إِلَى مُسَاعَدَةٍ.
أُرِيدُ takes what you want straight after it, with -an if it has no الْـ: أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً.

examples.en: Have you got time today? (to a woman)
I like swimming a lot.
We need a map.

why.q_en: Why does سُؤَالٌ end in -un in عِنْدِي سُؤَالٌ, when I'm the one who has it?
why.a_en: Because in Arabic the question is the subject: "at me (is) a question". عِنْدِي says where the question is, so the question takes the subject's ending, -un.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "he has a car"?
selftest.why_en: -hu is "he", and the car is the subject, so it ends in -un.

selftest.q_en: Which verb needs إِلَى after it?
selftest.why_en: أَحْتَاجُ إِلَى is "I need". أُحِبُّ and أُرِيدُ take the noun straight after them.

selftest.q_en: Which says "I like tea"?
selftest.why_en: What you like comes straight after أُحِبُّ, with الْـ and -a.

leads_to.en: أُرِيدُ with a verb: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنَامَ.

lesson.arabic-routine-sequence.title_en: Telling a routine: ثُمَّ, عَادَةً, صَبَاحًا
lesson.arabic-routine-sequence.family_en: Words for order and for when
steps: To tell a routine, use present verbs and a few time words: أَسْتَيْقِظُ صَبَاحًا, I wake up in the morning.
وَ, "and", joins actions without saying which comes first. ثُمَّ, "then", puts them in order: أَدْرُسُ ثُمَّ أَنَامُ, I study, then I sleep.
Words for when often end in -an: صَبَاحًا, in the morning; مَسَاءً, in the evening.
عَادَةً, usually, and كُلَّ يَوْمٍ, every day, show it's a habit, not just today.
Keep the same person through the routine: أَسْتَيْقِظُ، ثُمَّ أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ، وَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ.

examples.en: I usually drink coffee in the morning.
I have lunch, then I sleep for a little while.
My father comes home in the evening.

why.q_en: Why do صَبَاحًا and مَسَاءً end in -an?
why.a_en: The -an ending can say when something happens: صَبَاحًا is "in the morning", مَسَاءً "in the evening". Without it, صَبَاح is just the word "morning".

selftest.q_en: Which word puts two actions in order?
selftest.why_en: ثُمَّ is "then". عَادَةً is "usually", and صَبَاحًا "in the morning".

selftest.q_en: What does مَسَاءً mean?
selftest.why_en: With -an it says when: in the evening. "Every evening" is كُلَّ مَسَاءٍ.

selftest.q_en: Which shows a habit?
selftest.why_en: كُلَّ يَوْمٍ is "every day". الْآنَ is "now", and غَدًا "tomorrow".

phrases_ar: أَسْتَيْقِظُ، ثُمَّ أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ، وَأَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْعَمَلِ

leads_to.en: Ordering events in the past.

lesson.arabic-digits-prices.title_en: Arabic digits, and asking a price: كَمِ السِّعْرُ؟
lesson.arabic-digits-prices.family_en: Two sets of digits, and how to ask what something costs
steps: Arabic has its own digits, shown in the table, and many Arabic texts use 0–9 instead. Learn to read both.
Words run from right to left, but a number's digits keep the order you know: ٤٧ is 47, never 74.
Said aloud, numbers like 13 and 47 put the units first: ٤٧ is سَبْعَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ, "seven and forty", and ١٣ is ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ, "three-ten". They're still written ٤٧ and ١٣.
To ask a price, say كَمِ السِّعْرُ؟, what's the price? or بِكَمْ هَذَا؟, how much is this?
A price comes with its currency: بِعَشَرَةِ جُنَيْهَاتٍ, for ten pounds. If you're not sure you heard it right, say it back as a question.
How a number changes the noun after it comes later. For now, learn prices as whole phrases.

examples.en: How much is this pen?
The pen costs three pounds.

words.en: for three (بِـ: at a price of)

examples.en: What's the price, please?

words.en: your kindness (-ka: to a man); with مِنْ, "please"

why.q_en: Arabic is written right to left, so why isn't ٤٧ read as 74?
why.a_en: Words go right to left, but numbers keep their digits in the order you know, with the biggest place on the left. So you read a number the same way in an Arabic sentence as in an English one: ٤٧ is 47.

selftest.q_en: What number is ٣٨?
selftest.why_en: The digits keep their order: ٣ is 3 and ٨ is 8, so ٣٨ is 38.

selftest.q_en: Which asks "How much is this?"
selftest.why_en: بِكَمْ is "for how much". أَيْنَ هَذَا؟ is "Where is this?", and مَا هَذَا؟ "What is this?"

selftest.q_en: The seller says بِخَمْسَةِ جُنَيْهَاتٍ. What's the price?
selftest.why_en: خَمْسَة is five, and جُنَيْهَات is pounds.

leads_to.en: How a number changes the noun after it.

lesson.arabic-clock-calendar.family_en: The hour is said as "the fourth", not "four"
steps: Ask كَمِ السَّاعَةُ؟, what time is it? The answer starts with السَّاعَةُ, then the hour.
The hour is said as "the fourth", "the fifth": السَّاعَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ is four o'clock, literally "the fourth hour". One o'clock is السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ, "the one hour".
These hour words end in ـَة because سَاعَة is feminine, and they match it.
