For half past, add وَالنِّصْفُ, "and the half"; for quarter past, وَالرُّبْعُ. Quarter to is إِلَّا رُبْعًا, "less a quarter", after the next hour.

"At" a time is فِي السَّاعَةِ, and the hour then ends in -i too: فِي السَّاعَةِ الرَّابِعَةِ, at four. Only the two-word hours, 11 and 12, never change: فِي السَّاعَةِ الثَّانِيَةَ عَشْرَةَ, at twelve.
Add the part of the day when it matters: صَبَاحًا, in the morning; بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ, in the afternoon; مَسَاءً, in the evening.

examples.en: What time is it now?
The lesson is at ten in the morning.
I'll arrive at half past six.

why.q_en: Why is four o'clock السَّاعَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ, and not أَرْبَعَة?
why.a_en: Arabic tells the time as "the fourth hour". أَرْبَعَة counts things: four books. الرَّابِعَة says which one in order, the fourth, so it takes الْـ and matches سَاعَة.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "It's five o'clock"?
selftest.why_en: The hour is "the fifth": الْخَامِسَةُ. خَمْسُ سَاعَاتٍ is "five hours".

selftest.q_en: What does وَالنِّصْفُ add to a time?
selftest.why_en: نِصْف is "half". Quarter past is وَالرُّبْعُ, and quarter to إِلَّا رُبْعًا.

selftest.q_en: Which says "at seven"?
selftest.why_en: After فِي, both words end in -i, and the hour is "the seventh".

leads_to.en: Suggesting a day to meet, and confirming it.

lesson.arabic-clock-calendar.title_en: Days of the week, and "on" a day: يَوْمَ الْأَحَدِ
lesson.arabic-clock-calendar.family_en: Each day is "the day of …", and most are named after numbers
steps: Each day is "the day of …": يَوْمُ الْأَحَدِ, Sunday. You can also leave out يَوْمُ and say just الْأَحَدُ.
Sunday to Thursday are named after numbers, because the week is counted from Sunday: الْأَحَد is "one", and الْخَمِيس "five".
To say "on" a day, you don't need a word for "on": يَوْمَ, with -a, does the job. أُسَافِرُ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ, I'm travelling on Thursday.
Usually the day comes first, then the time: يَوْمَ الْأَحَدِ فِي السَّاعَةِ الْعَاشِرَةِ, on Sunday at ten.
When a day and a time both matter, say them back to check: either one can be misheard.

examples.en: Today is Thursday.
I have an appointment on Wednesday.
I don't work on Saturday.

why.q_en: Why is it يَوْمَ, with -a, in عِنْدِي مَوْعِدٌ يَوْمَ الْأَرْبِعَاءِ, but يَوْمُ in the table?
why.a_en: In the table, يَوْمُ الْأَرْبِعَاءِ is just the day's name. When the day says when something happens, يَوْمَ takes -a, meaning "on that day", so Arabic needs no separate word for "on".

selftest.q_en: Which day is يَوْمُ الْخَمِيسِ?
selftest.why_en: الْخَمِيس comes from "five": the fifth day, counting from Sunday.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "on Sunday"?
selftest.why_en: الْأَحَد comes from "one": the first day. يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ is "on Saturday", and يَوْمَ الِاثْنَيْنِ "on Monday".

selftest.q_en: What does the -a on يَوْمَ add in أُسَافِرُ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ?
selftest.why_en: يَوْمَ with -a says when: on Thursday. "Every Thursday" would be كُلَّ يَوْمِ خَمِيسٍ.

leads_to.en: Suggesting a day to meet, and confirming it.

lesson.arabic-directions-map.title_en: Where it is, and how to get there: بِجَانِبِ, اِذْهَبْ يَمِينًا
lesson.arabic-directions-map.family_en: Place words say where something is; commands say how to get there
steps: There are two kinds of sentence here: where a place is, and how to get there. Keep them apart.
Where: the place, then أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ or بِجَانِبِ, then a landmark ending in -i: الْبَيْتُ خَلْفَ الْحَدِيقَةِ, the house is behind the park.
How to get there: a command. اِذْهَبْ is "go" to a man, and اِذْهَبِي to a woman.
The way to go ends in -an: يَمِينًا, right; يَسَارًا, left; مُسْتَقِيمًا, straight on.
Follow one step at a time. If you lose the way, ask again from the last place you're sure of.

examples.en: The restaurant is in front of the hotel.
Go straight on, then left.
The station is on the right.

why.q_en: Why is it يَمِينًا in اِذْهَبْ يَمِينًا, but الْيَمِينِ in عَلَى الْيَمِينِ?
why.a_en: They do different jobs. يَمِينًا, with -an, says which way to go. عَلَى الْيَمِينِ says where something is, "on the right", and after عَلَى the word ends in -i.

selftest.q_en: Which means "behind"?
selftest.why_en: أَمَامَ is "in front of", and بِجَانِبِ "next to".

selftest.q_en: How do you tell a woman "Go left"?
selftest.why_en: To a woman the command is اِذْهَبِي, and يَسَارًا is "left".

selftest.q_en: Which sentence says where something is, not how to get there?
selftest.why_en: It uses أَمَامَ to say where the bakery is. The other two are commands: how to get there.

leads_to.en: How commands like اِذْهَبْ are made, and "don't".

lesson.arabic-food-shopping.title_en: In a shop: asking for things, and understanding the reply
lesson.arabic-food-shopping.family_en: Polite requests, and the seller's answers

table.en: here you are; please, go ahead
here you are; please, go ahead

steps: A shop visit has a few steps: ask for something, check they have it, ask the price, and say thank you.
Ask with أُرِيدُ and the thing, ending in -an when it has no الْـ: أُرِيدُ شَايًا, I'd like some tea. Then add "please".
"Please" changes with who you're talking to: مِنْ فَضْلِكَ to a man, مِنْ فَضْلِكِ to a woman. Only the last vowel changes.
Listen for the reply. تَفَضَّلْ, here you are, means they have it. لَيْسَ عِنْدَنَا, we haven't got any, means you'll need something else.
Describing words match the thing: الْخُبْزُ رَخِيصٌ, the bread is cheap, but الْقَهْوَةُ رَخِيصَةٌ, the coffee is cheap.

examples.en: I'd like a kilo of apples, please.

words.en: your kindness (-ka: to a man); with مِنْ, "please"

examples.en: Have you got fresh bread?
That's very expensive.

why.q_en: Why is "expensive" غَالٍ, with no ي at the end?
why.a_en: The word ends in a long ī, but with the -in ending and no الْـ, that ī drops: you write and say غَالٍ. With الْـ it comes back: الْغَالِي, the expensive one. For a feminine word, it's غَالِيَة.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "please" to a woman?
selftest.why_en: To a woman, the last vowel is -i: فَضْلِكِ. مِنْ فَضْلِكَ is to a man, and تَفَضَّلْ is something else: see the next question.

selftest.q_en: The seller hands you the bread and says تَفَضَّلْ. What does it mean here?
selftest.why_en: تَفَضَّلْ offers something: here you are, or please go ahead. "Thank you" is شُكْرًا.

selftest.q_en: Which is the opposite of غَالٍ?
selftest.why_en: غَالٍ is "expensive", and رَخِيص "cheap". جَدِيد is "new", and كَبِير "big".

leads_to.en: Comparing two things: أَكْبَرُ مِنْ, bigger than.

lesson.arabic-messages-needs.title_en: Short messages: أَنَا مُتَأَخِّرٌ, أَنَا آسِفَةٌ
lesson.arabic-messages-needs.family_en: Saying what's happening and what you need, simply

table.en: I'll be there in ten minutes

steps: A short message says what's happening, then what comes next. Simple sentences you're sure of work better than long ones.
Words describing yourself change if you're a woman: أَنَا مُتَأَخِّرَةٌ, أَنَا آسِفَةٌ, with ـَة.
Verbs with أَـ don't change: أَصِلُ, I arrive, is the same for a man or a woman.
لَا before a present verb makes it "not": لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ, I can't. A missing لَا turns the message round, so check for it.

examples.en: I'm sorry, the bus is late. (a woman writing)
I'm waiting for you at the station.

words.en: I'm waiting for you (-ka: you, a man)

examples.en: My phone isn't working.

why.q_en: Why مُتَأَخِّرَةٌ for الْحَافِلَةُ? A bus isn't a woman.
why.a_en: In Arabic every noun is masculine or feminine, and a describing word matches it. حَافِلَة ends in ـَة, so it's feminine, and "late" becomes مُتَأَخِّرَةٌ.

selftest.q_en: A woman writes "I'm late". Which is right?
selftest.why_en: A woman adds ـَة to the describing word. أَنْتِ مُتَأَخِّرَةٌ is "you're late", to a woman.

selftest.q_en: What does لَا do in لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ?
selftest.why_en: لَا before a present verb is "not": لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ, I can't.

selftest.q_en: Which stays the same whether a man or a woman writes it?
selftest.why_en: A verb with أَـ is the same for both. آسِف and مُتَأَخِّر add ـَة for a woman.

leads_to.en: لَا, and the other words for "not".

lesson.arabic-a1-listening.title_en: Listening for the details: name, job, place
lesson.arabic-a1-listening.family_en: What to listen for when someone introduces themselves
steps: In a short introduction, listen for three things: the name, the job and the place.
Each has its signal: a name comes after اِسْمِي, a job after أَنَا, and a place after مِنْ or فِي.
A job ending in ـَة tells you a woman is speaking or being spoken about: مُهَنْدِس, مُهَنْدِسَة.
Listen once without the text, then a second time to check. If you're not sure of something, write a question mark rather than a guess.

examples.en: My name is Laylā, and I'm a teacher.
I work in a hospital in Cairo.

examples.ar: هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ أَسْمَعَ الْمُحَادَثَةَ مَرَّتَيْنِ؟
examples.en: Can I hear the conversation twice?

why.q_en: Why is "twice" مَرَّتَيْنِ?
why.a_en: مَرَّة is "one time". For two of anything Arabic has its own ending: the ـَة becomes ـَتَيْنِ, so مَرَّتَيْنِ is "two times", with no separate word for "two".

selftest.q_en: You hear أَنَا طَبِيبَةٌ. What do you learn?
selftest.why_en: طَبِيبَة is a doctor, and the ـَة shows it's a woman.

selftest.q_en: Which word means "twice"?
selftest.why_en: مَرَّة is "once", and مَرَّات "times". The ـَتَيْنِ ending makes it two.

selftest.q_en: You didn't catch the speaker's job. What should you write?
choices: a question mark, then listen again
selftest.answer: a question mark, then listen again
selftest.why_en: Mark what you're not sure of. A guess from what seems likely isn't what you heard.

leads_to.en: Following a longer account you hear.

lesson.arabic-a1-reading.family_en: Short words on doors and notices, and the verbs they come from
steps: A sign is short. Read it for what it tells you to do; you don't need to work out every ending.
Many sign words come from a verb you may know: مَدْخَل, entrance, is from دَخَلَ, to go in, and مَخْرَج, exit, from خَرَجَ, to go out.
On a sign, words are usually read without their endings, as if you paused after each one. This card shows the endings in full.
Answer from what the sign says, not from what seems likely: مُغْلَق says closed, but not why or until when.

examples.en: The museum is open from nine o'clock.
The exit is on the left.
The pharmacy is closed today.

why.q_en: Why do مَدْخَل and دَخَلَ look alike?
why.a_en: They share the letters د-خ-ل, which carry the idea of going in. Arabic builds many words from three letters like these: دَخَلَ, he went in; مَدْخَل, a way in.

selftest.q_en: A shop door says مُغْلَق. What does it mean?
selftest.why_en: مُغْلَق is "closed". "Open" is مَفْتُوح.

selftest.q_en: Which sign shows the way out?
selftest.why_en: مَخْرَج comes from خَرَجَ, to go out. مَدْخَل is the way in, and مَمْنُوع "not allowed".

selftest.q_en: A sign says الْمَكْتَبُ مُغْلَقٌ. What does it tell you?
choices: the office is closed because of a holiday
selftest.why_en: It says only that the office is closed, not why or until when.

leads_to.en: Why مَدْخَل and دَخَلَ look alike: roots and patterns.

lesson.arabic-a1-speaking.title_en: Keeping a conversation going: وَأَنْتَ؟, أَيْضًا, طَبْعًا
lesson.arabic-a1-speaking.family_en: Short words that turn a speech into a conversation
steps: A conversation is more than a speech: answer, then ask back. وَأَنْتَ؟ after your answer passes the turn: أَنَا مِنْ تُونِسَ، وَأَنْتَ؟
To a woman, it's وَأَنْتِ؟. Only the last vowel changes.
Short words keep it going: طَبْعًا, of course; رُبَّمَا, maybe; حَسَنًا, all right.
أَيْضًا, too, goes after what it adds to: وَأَنَا أَيْضًا, me too.

examples.en: I work in a bank, and you?

examples.ar: هَلْ تُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ؟ طَبْعًا، كُلَّ يَوْمٍ.
examples.en: Do you like coffee? Of course, every day.
Maybe I'll travel tomorrow. See you!

why.q_en: Why do طَبْعًا and حَسَنًا end in -an?
why.a_en: Many words that say how or when end in -an, like غَدًا, tomorrow, and صَبَاحًا, in the morning. طَبْعًا is literally "naturally", and حَسَنًا "well, fine". Learn them as they are.

selftest.q_en: A woman tells you where she's from. How do you ask her back?
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "and you?" is وَأَنْتِ؟. وَأَنْتَ؟ is to a man.

selftest.q_en: What does رُبَّمَا mean?
selftest.why_en: رُبَّمَا is "maybe". "Of course" is طَبْعًا, and "all right" حَسَنًا.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "me too"?
selftest.why_en: أَيْضًا goes after what it adds to. وَأَنْتَ أَيْضًا is "you too".

leads_to.en: A conversation with a goal: sorting something out.

lesson.arabic-a1-writing.title_en: Writing about yourself: عُمْرِي, أَعْمَلُ, أَتَكَلَّمُ
lesson.arabic-a1-writing.family_en: A short profile: age, work, family, languages
steps: Short sentences are fine: one fact each, joined with وَ when they belong together.

Keep the speaker the same all the way through: a woman writes أَنَا مُتَزَوِّجَةٌ, with ـَة, and every word that describes her takes ـَة too. Verbs with أَـ, like أَعْمَلُ, stay the same for everyone.
For your age, write عُمْرِي, my age, then the number and سَنَةً: learn it as a phrase for now.
Write what you mean first, then compare with a model and fix one or two things.

examples.en: I'm twenty-five.
I'm married, and I have a son.
I speak Arabic and English.

why.q_en: Why سَنَةً, "year", in عُمْرِي عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً, and not "years"?
why.a_en: After the numbers 11 to 99, Arabic uses the singular, ending in -an: عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً is literally "twenty year". It's a fixed rule, so learn the phrase whole for now.

selftest.q_en: A woman writes "I'm married". Which is right?
selftest.why_en: A woman adds ـَة. أَنْتِ مُتَزَوِّجَةٌ is "you're married", to a woman.

selftest.q_en: What does عُمْرِي mean?
selftest.why_en: عُمْر is "age", and the ـِي is "my". "My hobby" is هِوَايَتِي.

selftest.q_en: Which says "I speak two languages"?
selftest.why_en: ـَتَيْنِ makes two, and أَـ is "I". يَتَكَلَّمُ is "he speaks".

leads_to.en: Linking sentences with a reason and a result.

lesson.arabic-past-suffixes.title_en: Past verbs: the ending shows who (ذَهَبْتُ, ذَهَبَتْ)
lesson.arabic-past-suffixes.family_en: In the past, who did it goes on the end of the verb
steps: In the present, a letter in front shows who. In the past, it's an ending: ذَهَبْتُ, I went.
The plain form, ذَهَبَ, is "he". It's also the form a dictionary gives.
Watch the last vowel: ـْتُ is "I", ـْتَ is "you" to a man, and ـْتِ is "you" to a woman. ـَتْ is "she".
Without vowel marks, these four look the same: ذَهَبْتُ, ذَهَبْتَ, ذَهَبْتِ, ذَهَبَتْ. The sentence tells you which.
For groups, ـْنَا is "we" and ـُوا is "they": ذَهَبْنَا, ذَهَبُوا.

examples.en: Yesterday we went to the market.
Did you understand the lesson? (to a woman)

words.en: did you understand (ـْتِ: you, a woman)

examples.en: Salmā came back home.

why.q_en: Why is there an alif at the end of ذَهَبُوا that isn't said?
why.a_en: It's a spelling rule: the -ū ending for "they" is written with an extra alif after the و. It's silent, and only marks the end of the verb.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I understood"?
selftest.why_en: ـْتُ is "I". فَهِمْتَ is "you understood" (to a man), and فَهِمَتْ "she understood".

selftest.q_en: Which ending means "we"?
selftest.why_en: ـْنَا is "we": ذَهَبْنَا. ـُوا is "they", and ـَتْ "she".

selftest.q_en: You ask a woman "Did you drink tea?" Which is right?
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "you" ends in ـْتِ. شَرِبْتَ is to a man, and شَرِبْتُ "I drank".

leads_to.en: Asking about the past.
Past verbs with a long ā in the middle, and where it goes: قَالَ, قُلْتُ.

lesson.arabic-past-questions.title_en: Asking about the past: مَاذَا فَعَلْتَ؟
lesson.arabic-past-questions.family_en: A question word, then the past verb, and an answer with ـْتُ

table.en: Where did you go? (to a woman)

steps: Put the question word first, then the past verb: أَيْنَ ذَهَبْتِ؟, where did you go?
There's no extra word like English "did": the past verb does it all.
To answer, keep the verb and change "you" to "I": the question's ـْتَ or ـْتِ becomes ـْتُ. مَتَى رَجَعْتَ؟, when did you come back? رَجَعْتُ أَمْسِ, I came back yesterday.
Answer what was asked: أَيْنَ wants a place, مَتَى a time, and مَعَ مَنْ a person.

examples.en: Who did you go to the restaurant with?
Why did you come back early? (to a woman)

words.en: did you come back (ـْتِ: a woman)

examples.en: I found my key under the chair.

why.q_en: Why does مَعَ مَنْ, "with whom", come first, when English says "Who did you go with?"
why.a_en: In Arabic the question word comes first, and any small word that goes with it comes along: مَعَ مَنْ, with whom. English can leave "with" at the end; Arabic can't.

selftest.q_en: Someone asks أَيْنَ ذَهَبْتَ؟ Which answer fits?
selftest.why_en: أَيْنَ asks for a place, and the answer is about "I": ذَهَبْتُ. ذَهَبْتُ أَمْسِ gives a time, and ذَهَبْتَ is "you went".

selftest.q_en: What does لِمَاذَا ask for?
selftest.why_en: لِمَاذَا is "why". A time is مَتَى, and a place أَيْنَ.

selftest.q_en: How do you ask "What happened?"
selftest.why_en: مَاذَا asks "what". مَتَى حَدَثَ؟ is "When did it happen?", and أَيْنَ حَدَثَ؟ "Where did it happen?"

leads_to.en: Saying what didn't happen, with لَمْ.

lesson.arabic-kana-background.family_en: كَانَ puts a description into the past
steps: Arabic needs no "is" in the present: الشَّارِعُ هَادِئٌ, the street is quiet. For the past, add كَانَ: كَانَ الشَّارِعُ هَادِئًا, the street was quiet.
After كَانَ, the describing word ends in -an: هَادِئًا, not هَادِئٌ. The thing described keeps its -u.

كَانَ takes the past endings: كَانَتْ, she was; كُنْتُ, I was. Before an ending that starts with a consonant (ـْتُ, ـْتَ, ـْتِ, ـْنَا), its long ā turns into a short u: كَانَ, but كُنْتُ. Before ـَتْ and ـُوا it stays: كَانَتْ, كَانُوا.
كَانَ with a present verb means "was doing" or "used to do": كُنْتُ أَعْمَلُ فِي مَطْعَمٍ. The context tells you which.

examples.en: The restaurant was closed on Friday.
Were you tired yesterday? (to a woman)

examples.ar: كُنَّا نَلْعَبُ فِي الْحَدِيقَةِ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ.
examples.en: We used to play in the park every day.

why.q_en: Why does هَادِئٌ become هَادِئًا after كَانَ?
why.a_en: كَانَ changes the ending of the word that describes. Without it, الشَّارِعُ هَادِئٌ has two -u endings. With كَانَ, the describing word takes -an: كَانَ الشَّارِعُ هَادِئًا.

selftest.q_en: A man says "I was tired". Which is right?
selftest.why_en: ـْتُ is "I", and after كَانَ the describing word ends in -an. كَانَ مُتْعَبًا is "he was tired".

selftest.q_en: Which says "The room was quiet"?
selftest.why_en: The room keeps -u and the describing word takes -an. كَانَتْ is "she" or a feminine "it"; its sukūn becomes -i before الْـ.

selftest.q_en: What can كُنْتُ أَعْمَلُ mean?
choices: I was working, or I used to work
selftest.answer: I was working, or I used to work
selftest.why_en: كَانَ with a present verb is "was doing" or "used to do".

leads_to.en: كَانَ's sisters: أَصْبَحَ, لَيْسَ, مَا زَالَ.

lesson.arabic-story-connectors.title_en: Putting events in order: أَوَّلًا, ثُمَّ, أَخِيرًا
lesson.arabic-story-connectors.family_en: Words for first, then, before, after, when and because
steps: وَ just adds one event to another. To show the order, use أَوَّلًا, first; ثُمَّ, then; and أَخِيرًا, finally.
قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ take a noun, which ends in -i: قَبْلَ الدَّرْسِ, before the lesson.
بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ, after that, stands on its own and points back to the last event.
عِنْدَمَا, when, takes a whole sentence: عِنْدَمَا وَصَلْتُ، كَانَ الْبَابُ مُغْلَقًا, when I arrived, the door was closed.
لِأَنَّ, because, gives the reason: بَقِيتُ فِي الْبَيْتِ لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ كَانَ بَارِدًا, I stayed at home because it was cold.

examples.ar: أَوَّلًا شَرِبْتُ الْقَهْوَةَ، ثُمَّ قَرَأْتُ الْجَرِيدَةَ.
examples.en: First I drank the coffee, then I read the newspaper.
Before the trip, I visited my grandmother.
And at last the train arrived.

why.q_en: What's the difference between بَعْدَ and بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ?
why.a_en: بَعْدَ needs a noun after it: بَعْدَ الْعَمَلِ, after work. بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ, literally "after that", needs nothing more: it points back to what you just said.

selftest.q_en: Which word starts a list of events?
selftest.why_en: أَوَّلًا is "first". أَخِيرًا is "finally", and ثُمَّ "then".

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "after the lesson"?
selftest.why_en: بَعْدَ comes first, and the noun after it ends in -i.

selftest.q_en: What comes after عِنْدَمَا?
selftest.why_en: عِنْدَمَا, when, takes a whole sentence: عِنْدَمَا وَصَلْتُ, when I arrived.

phrases_ar: بَقِيتُ فِي الْبَيْتِ لِأَنَّ الْجَوَّ كَانَ بَارِدًا

leads_to.en: More words for reasons and purposes.

lesson.arabic-story-retell.title_en: Telling a story: ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ, فِي الْبِدَايَةِ, فِي النِّهَايَةِ
lesson.arabic-story-retell.family_en: How to open, move along and close a short story
steps: Open with ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ, one day, or فِي الْبِدَايَةِ, at the beginning, and close with فِي النِّهَايَةِ, in the end.
A story about someone else uses he and she: ذَهَبَ, he went; ذَهَبَتْ, she went.
Stories often put the verb first: ذَهَبَ سَامِي إِلَى الْبَحْرِ, Sāmī went to the sea.
To retell a story, keep its people, its events and their order, in your own words. Don't add what the story doesn't say.

examples.ar: ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ، ذَهَبَ سَامِي إِلَى الْبَحْرِ.
examples.en: One day, Sāmī went to the sea.

examples.ar: فِي الْبِدَايَةِ سَبَحَ قَلِيلًا، ثُمَّ نَامَ عَلَى الرَّمْلِ.
examples.en: At first he swam a little, then he slept on the sand.

examples.ar: فِي النِّهَايَةِ رَجَعَ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ سَعِيدًا.
examples.en: In the end, he went back home happy.

why.q_en: Why does the verb come before the name in ذَهَبَ سَامِي?
why.a_en: Arabic often starts a sentence about what happened with the verb: ذَهَبَ سَامِي, literally "went Sāmī". You can also start with the name, سَامِي ذَهَبَ, but stories usually lead with the verb.

selftest.q_en: Which phrase starts a story?
selftest.why_en: ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ is "one day". فِي النِّهَايَةِ is "in the end", and مُلَخَّص "a summary".

selftest.q_en: You're retelling Salmā's story: she went to the market. Which is right?
selftest.why_en: Salmā is "she", so the verb ends in ـَتْ, even when it comes first.

selftest.q_en: A story says ذَهَبَتْ لَيْلَى إِلَى السُّوقِ وَاشْتَرَتْ خُبْزًا. Which retelling keeps to the story?
choices: Laylā went to the market and bought bread
Laylā went to the market because she was hungry
Laylā went to the market with her mother
selftest.answer: Laylā went to the market and bought bread
selftest.why_en: The story doesn't say why she went, or who with. Don't add it.

phrases_ar: ذَهَبَتْ لَيْلَى إِلَى السُّوقِ وَاشْتَرَتْ خُبْزًا

leads_to.en: Reporting what someone said.

lesson.arabic-a1-portfolio.title_en: Talking about your learning: أَتَعَلَّمُ, قَوِيّ, ضَعِيف, هَدَفِي
lesson.arabic-a1-portfolio.family_en: Words for what you're learning, how it's going, and what comes next
steps: أَتَعَلَّمُ is "I learn" or "I'm learning": أَتَعَلَّمُ الْعَرَبِيَّةَ. The أ in front means "I", as in every present verb.
To say how a skill is going, add ـِي, "my", to the skill, then say قَوِيّ, strong, or ضَعِيف, weak: قِرَاءَتِي قَوِيَّةٌ, my reading is strong.
قِرَاءَة and كِتَابَة end in ـَة, so the describing word takes ـَة too. Before ـِي, the ـَة is written ت: قِرَاءَتِي.
Pick your next goal from your weakest skill: هَدَفِي الِاسْتِمَاعُ, my goal is listening.

examples.en: I've been learning Arabic for three months.
My listening is weak, and I need some review.
My progress in reading is good.

why.q_en: Why قَوِيَّةٌ for my reading, but ضَعِيفٌ for my listening?
why.a_en: The describing word matches the skill's word. قِرَاءَة ends in ـَة, so it's feminine: قِرَاءَتِي قَوِيَّةٌ. اِسْتِمَاع has no ـَة, so it's masculine: اِسْتِمَاعِي ضَعِيفٌ.

selftest.q_en: Which says "My writing is strong"?
selftest.why_en: كِتَابَة ends in ـَة, so قَوِيّ takes ـَة too. كِتَابِي is "my book".

selftest.q_en: What does أَتَعَلَّمُ mean?
selftest.why_en: أَتَعَلَّمُ is "I learn, I'm learning". "I teach" is أُعَلِّمُ, and "I know" أَعْرِفُ.

selftest.q_en: Listening is your weakest skill. Which goal fits?
selftest.why_en: Pick the next goal from your weakest skill: here, listening.

leads_to.en: Describing your level, and your next step.

lesson.arabic-future-plans.title_en: Talking about the future: سَـ and سَوْفَ
lesson.arabic-future-plans.family_en: "Will" goes in front of a present verb
steps: For the future, put سَـ on the front of a present verb: أَذْهَبُ, I go; سَأَذْهَبُ, I'll go.
سَوْفَ does the same as a separate word before the verb: سَوْفَ أَذْهَبُ. Both mean "will".
The verb doesn't change: سَـ goes in front of whichever present form you need: سَنَذْهَبُ, we'll go; سَتَذْهَبِينَ, you'll go (to a woman).
Add a time to make the plan clear: سَأُسَافِرُ الْأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِمَ, I'll travel next week. Like صَبَاحًا, a time like this takes the -a ending: -a here because of الْـ, -an without it.
A plan isn't a promise, and it isn't a wish either: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُسَافِرَ, I want to travel, says only what you'd like.

examples.en: We'll visit my grandmother the day after tomorrow.
Will you work on Saturday? (to a woman)

examples.ar: أَنْوِي أَنْ أَزُورَ مِصْرَ هَذَا الصَّيْفَ.
examples.en: I intend to visit Egypt this summer.

why.q_en: Why is سَـ joined to the verb, but سَوْفَ written apart?
why.a_en: سَـ is a single letter, and one-letter words in Arabic join the next word, like وَ and بِـ. سَوْفَ is a whole word, so it stands on its own. They mean the same.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I'll travel"?
selftest.why_en: سَـ in front makes it future. سَافَرْتُ is "I travelled", and أُسَافِرُ "I travel".

selftest.q_en: What does الْأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِمَ mean?
selftest.why_en: الْقَادِم is "the coming one". "Every week" is كُلَّ أُسْبُوعٍ.

selftest.q_en: Which says "We'll go"?
selftest.why_en: سَوْفَ and سَـ go with the present form, نَذْهَبُ, never the past.

leads_to.en: Plans that depend on something: إِذَا and إِنْ.

lesson.arabic-negation-system.family_en: Four words for "not", each with its own time and its own verb ending

table.en: I don't travel, I'm not travelling

steps: Arabic has several words for "not", and each goes with its own time: لَا for now, لَمْ for the past, لَنْ for the future.
After لَمْ and لَنْ, use the present form of the verb, even for the past: لَمْ أُسَافِرْ, I didn't travel.
The verb's last vowel changes: after لَمْ it becomes a sukūn, أُسَافِرْ; after لَنْ it becomes -a, أُسَافِرَ. Endings in ـِينَ and ـُونَ drop their نَ instead: لَمْ تُسَافِرِي, لَنْ تُسَافِرُوا.
لَيْسَ is for sentences with no verb: الْمَطْعَمُ مَفْتُوحٌ, the restaurant is open; لَيْسَ الْمَطْعَمُ مَفْتُوحًا, it isn't open. Like كَانَ, it gives the describing word -an.
لَيْسَ changes for who: لَسْتُ, I'm not; لَسْتَ, you're not (to a man); لَيْسَتْ, she isn't.

examples.en: I haven't eaten anything today.
We won't travel this summer.
She isn't at home now.

why.q_en: Why أُسَافِرْ, a present form, after لَمْ, when the meaning is past?
why.a_en: That's how Arabic says "didn't": لَمْ takes the present form, shortens its ending, and turns the meaning into the past. لَمْ never goes with a past verb.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I won't travel"?
selftest.why_en: لَنْ is for the future. لَمْ أُسَافِرْ is "I didn't travel", and لَا أُسَافِرُ "I don't travel".

selftest.q_en: Which word says "not" in a sentence with no verb?
selftest.why_en: لَيْسَ goes with sentences like الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ. لَمْ and لَنْ need a verb.

selftest.q_en: A man says "I'm not tired". Which is right?
selftest.why_en: لَسْتُ is "I'm not", and the describing word takes -an. لَيْسَ مُتْعَبًا is "he isn't tired".

leads_to.en: لَمْ with كَانَ: لَمْ يَكُنْ.
What the endings after لَنْ and لَمْ are called, and the other words that call for them.

lesson.arabic-requests-imperatives.title_en: Telling someone what to do: اِفْتَحْ, اُدْخُلْ, لَا تَتَأَخَّرْ
lesson.arabic-requests-imperatives.family_en: Commands come from the present verb; "don't" comes from لَا
steps: A command starts from the "you" present verb: drop the تَـ or تُـ in front, and the last vowel. تَفْتَحُ, you open, becomes اِفْتَحْ, open!

If the word would then start with two consonants, add a helping vowel. When the "you" form starts with تَـ, it's اُ if the present has u in the middle (تَدْخُلُ, اُدْخُلْ), otherwise اِ (اِفْتَحْ, اِجْلِسْ). When it starts with تُـ, like تُغْلِقُ, the helper is a real hamza, أَ, always said: أَغْلِقْ, close!
The ending changes with who you're telling: ـِي to a woman (اِفْتَحِي), ـُوا to a group (اِفْتَحُوا).
"Don't" is لَا with the "you" present form, its last vowel dropped: لَا تَتَأَخَّرْ, don't be late. It is never لَا with the command.
A bare command can sound abrupt. Add مِنْ فَضْلِكَ, please, or ask instead: هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تَفْتَحَ الْبَابَ؟, could you open the door?

examples.en: Come in and sit down, please.
Close the window, please. (to a woman)
Don't wait here. (to a group)

why.q_en: Why اُدْخُلْ with اُ, but اِجْلِسْ with اِ?
why.a_en: The helping vowel follows the middle vowel of the present: تَدْخُلُ has u, so اُدْخُلْ; تَجْلِسُ has i, so اِجْلِسْ. When the middle vowel is a, it's اِ too: تَفْتَحُ, اِفْتَحْ.

selftest.q_en: How do you tell a woman "Sit down"?
selftest.why_en: To a woman, a command ends in ـِي. اِجْلِسْ is to a man, and تَجْلِسِينَ is "you sit".

selftest.q_en: Which means "Don't wait!" to a man?
selftest.why_en: "Don't" is لَا with the "you" form, its last vowel dropped. لَا تَنْتَظِرُ is "you don't wait".

selftest.q_en: The present of خَرَجَ, to go out, is يَخْرُجُ. What's the command to a man?
selftest.why_en: The present has u in the middle, so the helping vowel is اُ.

leads_to.en: Asking instead of telling: هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تَفْتَحَ؟

lesson.arabic-modal-complements.title_en: Want to, can, must: أَنْ and the verb after it
lesson.arabic-modal-complements.family_en: A frame, then أَنْ, then a present verb ending in -a
steps: Words like "want", "can" and "must" take أَنْ, then a present verb: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنَامَ, I want to sleep.
After أَنْ, the verb's last vowel becomes -a: أَنَامُ, but أَنْ أَنَامَ.
Both verbs change for who: تُرِيدُ أَنْ تَنَامَ, you want to sleep. يَجِبُ and يُمْكِنُ stay the same: يَجِبُ أَنْ تَذْهَبَ, you must go.
Endings in ـِينَ and ـُونَ lose their نَ after أَنْ: تَنَامِينَ, but يَجِبُ أَنْ تَنَامِي; تَنَامُونَ, but أَنْ تَنَامُوا, with a silent alif.
English "can" isn't always أَسْتَطِيعُ. To ask if something is possible or allowed, use يُمْكِنُ: هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ أَجْلِسَ هُنَا؟, can I sit here?

examples.ar: لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ أَنَامَ فِي الطَّائِرَةِ.
examples.en: I can't sleep on the plane.
You must go to bed early. (to a woman)

words.en: you sleep (to a woman; no نَ after أَنْ)

examples.en: I try to read every day.

why.q_en: Why أَنَامَ, with -a, after أَنْ, when it's أَنَامُ on its own?
why.a_en: أَنْ changes the verb's last vowel to -a. It marks the verb as the thing wanted, possible or needed, rather than a plain statement of fact.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I want to sleep"?
selftest.why_en: أُرِيدُ takes أَنْ, and after أَنْ the verb ends in -a.

selftest.q_en: A woman is told "You must go". Which is right?
selftest.why_en: يَجِبُ doesn't change, and ـِينَ loses its نَ after أَنْ.

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "Can I sit here?"
selftest.why_en: يُمْكِنُ needs أَنْ, and the verb after أَنْ ends in -a.

leads_to.en: The -a ending after لِكَيْ, "so that", too.

lesson.arabic-plans-dialogue.title_en: Making a plan together: مَا رَأْيُكَ؟, لِلْأَسَفِ, إِذَنْ

table.en: What do you think? (to a man)

steps: Planning together has four moves: suggest, answer, change if needed, and confirm.
Suggest with a question: هَلْ نَلْتَقِي غَدًا؟, shall we meet tomorrow? The present نَلْتَقِي, we meet, works for a plan.
If you can't, say so clearly and give a reason. لِلْأَسَفِ, unfortunately, makes it a no, not a maybe.
Offer something else with بَدَلًا مِنْ, instead of, and ask مَا رَأْيُكَ؟, what do you think?
Finish with إِذَنْ, so, and say the agreed day, time and place again: إِذَنْ نَلْتَقِي يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ فِي الْمَقْهَى.

examples.ar: هَلْ نَلْتَقِي يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ؟
examples.en: Shall we meet on Thursday afternoon?
Unfortunately, I have a lesson on Thursday.

examples.ar: إِذَنْ نَلْتَقِي يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ فِي الْمَقْهَى.
examples.en: So we'll meet on Friday at the café.

why.q_en: Why نَلْتَقِي, a present verb, for a plan in the future?
why.a_en: The present often covers plans that are already settled, as English does in "we're meeting on Friday". سَنَلْتَقِي, we'll meet, is right too.

selftest.q_en: Which reply is a clear no?
selftest.why_en: "Unfortunately, I can't." طَبْعًا is "of course", and أَنَا مُوَافِقٌ "I agree".

selftest.q_en: What does إِذَنْ do in إِذَنْ نَلْتَقِي يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ?
choices: it sums up what you've agreed
selftest.answer: it sums up what you've agreed
selftest.why_en: إِذَنْ is "so, then": it confirms the plan.

selftest.q_en: How do you ask a woman "What do you think?"
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "your" is ـكِ. رَأْيُكَ is to a man, and رَأْيِي is "my opinion".

phrases_ar: إِذَنْ نَلْتَقِي يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ فِي الْمَقْهَى

lesson.arabic-pronoun-attachment.title_en: One ending, three jobs: بَيْتُهُ, أَعْرِفُهُ, مَعَهُ
lesson.arabic-pronoun-attachment.family_en: The same endings mean "his", "him" or "with him", depending on the word they're on

table.en: I saw her, I saw it

steps: The endings ـهُ, ـهَا, ـنَا, ـهُمْ and the rest do three jobs, depending on the word they're on.

On a noun they mean "his", "her", "our": بَيْتُهُ, his house. On a verb they mean "him", "her", "us": أَعْرِفُهُ, I know him. After a small word like مَعَ, مِنْ or لِـ, they're who it's with, from or for: مَعَهُ, with him.
ـَة becomes ت before an ending: سَيَّارَة, but سَيَّارَتُهُ, his car.
Two small changes: لِـ, for, becomes لَـ before an ending (لَهُ, لَهَا, لَنَا), except لِي, for me; and "me" on a verb is ـنِي, while "my" on a noun is ـِي.
To look a word up, take the ending off first: نَعْرِفُهُمْ is نَعْرِفُ, we know, with ـهُمْ, them.

examples.en: I saw my friend and talked with her.
This present is for you.
I took the key from him yesterday.

why.q_en: Why مَعَهُ, with an ending, and not مَعَ with هُوَ?
why.a_en: After a small word like مَعَ, لِـ or مِنْ, "him" and "her" are always endings: مَعَهُ, لَهُ, مِنْهُ. هُوَ is only for the one the sentence is about: هُوَ مَعِي, he's with me.

selftest.q_en: What does ـهَا mean in سَيَّارَتُهَا?
selftest.why_en: On a noun, ـهَا is "her": her car. "For her" is لَهَا, and "with her" مَعَهَا.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I know them"?
selftest.why_en: ـهُمْ is "them". أَعْرِفُهُ is "I know him", and أَعْرِفُكُمْ "I know you all".

selftest.q_en: Which means "for us"?
selftest.why_en: لِـ with ـنَا is لَنَا. لَهُمْ is "for them", and مَعَنَا "with us".

leads_to.en: Taking the endings off to look a word up.

lesson.arabic-case-roles.title_en: Who did what: the endings -u, -a and -i
lesson.arabic-case-roles.family_en: In fully vowelled Arabic, a noun's ending shows its job
steps: In a fully vowelled sentence, the endings show each noun's job: -u for the doer, -a for what it's done to, -i after a small word like فِي.
Without الْـ, the endings double: -un, -an, -in. شَرِبَ وَلَدٌ حَلِيبًا, a boy drank milk.
Arabic grammar has names for these: فَاعِل, the doer, and مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ, what it's done to. The cases are مَرْفُوع (-u), مَنْصُوب (-a) and مَجْرُور (-i).
Work out the roles from the meaning first, then check the endings. Many texts leave the endings out, and some words never show them.

examples.en: The boy drank the milk in the kitchen.
The teacher opened the window.
Sāmī wrote a letter to his friend.

words.en: Sāmī (the doer; a name ending in ـِي shows no ending)

why.q_en: If the endings show who did what, can the words go in any order?
why.a_en: More freely than in English, yes: the endings keep the roles clear. But the usual order is the verb, then the doer, then the rest, and that's the safest one to use.

selftest.q_en: In فَتَحَتِ الْمُعَلِّمَةُ النَّافِذَةَ, which word is the doer?
selftest.why_en: It ends in -u: the teacher did the opening. النَّافِذَةَ, with -a, is what was opened.

selftest.q_en: What ending does a noun take after فِي?
selftest.why_en: After a small word like فِي, مِنْ or إِلَى, the noun ends in -i (or -in without الْـ).

selftest.q_en: What is a مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ?
choices: what the action is done to
selftest.answer: what the action is done to
selftest.why_en: مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ is what the action is done to, and it ends in -a. The doer is the فَاعِل.

leads_to.en: إِنَّ, which turns the -u of a subject into -a.

lesson.arabic-idafa-chains.title_en: Chains of nouns: مَكْتَبُ مُدِيرِ الْمَدْرَسَةِ
lesson.arabic-idafa-chains.family_en: "The … of the … of the …", and where a describing word goes
steps: Two nouns side by side mean "the … of …": بَابُ الْبَيْتِ, the door of the house.
You can chain more: مَكْتَبُ مُدِيرِ الْمَدْرَسَةِ, the office of the head of the school. Read it from the front: office, head, school.

Only the last noun can have الْـ; the others never take الْـ or -un. If the last noun is definite, with الْـ, a name or an ending like "my", the whole chain is definite: بَابُ الْبَيْتِ, the door of the house; سَيَّارَةُ أَبِي, my father's car.
Every noun after the first ends in -i. The first one's ending depends on its job in the sentence.
A describing word goes after the whole chain, and its ending usually shows which noun it describes: الْجَدِيدُ, with -u like بَيْتُ, is the house; الْجَدِيدِ, with -i, is the teacher.

examples.en: The bedroom window is open.
My sister works at Cairo University.
We lived in the town centre.

why.q_en: Why does بَيْتُ الْمُعَلِّمِ mean "the teacher's house" when بَيْت has no الْـ?
why.a_en: In a chain, the last noun makes the whole thing definite. Adding الْـ to بَيْت as well would be wrong: the first noun never takes it.

selftest.q_en: What does مَكْتَبُ مُدِيرِ الْمَدْرَسَةِ mean?
choices: the manager of the school office
selftest.why_en: Read from the front: the office of the head of the school.

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "the door of the room"?
selftest.why_en: The first noun has no الْـ, and the second ends in -i.

selftest.q_en: In بَيْتُ الْمُعَلِّمِ الْجَدِيدُ, what is new?
selftest.why_en: الْجَدِيدُ ends in -u, like بَيْتُ, so it describes the house.

lesson.arabic-dual-sound-plurals.title_en: Two of something, and plurals with endings: ـَانِ, ـُونَ, ـَات
lesson.arabic-dual-sound-plurals.family_en: A form for exactly two, and the plurals made by adding an ending

table.form_en: two, from a word in ـَة

steps: Arabic has a form for exactly two: add ـَانِ. طَالِب, a student; طَالِبَانِ, two students.
When the two are what the action is done to, or come after a small word like فِي or بَعْدَ, the ending is ـَيْنِ: اِشْتَرَيْتُ قَلَمَيْنِ, I bought two pens.
A word in ـَة keeps a ت: سَاعَة, سَاعَتَانِ.
Some words for people add ـُونَ for men or a mixed group, or ـِينَ when they're not the subject: مُهَنْدِسُونَ, مُهَنْدِسِينَ.
For women, the ending is ـَات: طَالِبَات. Where other nouns end in -a, ـَات ends in -i: رَأَيْتُ الطَّالِبَاتِ.
Most nouns don't use these endings: they change inside instead, like كِتَاب, كُتُب. Learn each plural with its word.

examples.en: We spent two days in Alexandria.
There are two old houses in our street.
Men and women engineers work at the company.

why.q_en: Why does بَيْتَانِ قَدِيمَانِ have the two-ending on both words?
why.a_en: A describing word matches its noun in number too. Two houses, so "old" takes the two-ending as well: بَيْتَانِ قَدِيمَانِ.

selftest.q_en: What does سَاعَتَانِ mean?
selftest.why_en: ـَانِ makes two, and the ة of سَاعَة stays as ت.

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "I visited two houses"?
selftest.why_en: The houses aren't the subject here, so the ending is ـَيْنِ, on the singular بَيْت.

selftest.q_en: Which plural ending is for a group of women?
selftest.why_en: ـُونَ is for men or a mixed group, and ـَانِ is for two.

leads_to.en: Three to ten with a noun.

lesson.arabic-quantity-comparison.family_en: One pattern for comparing, with مِنْ for "than"

table.en: The village is smaller than the town

steps: To compare, Arabic uses one pattern: أَ in front and the word's three root letters after it. كَبِير, big; أَكْبَر, bigger.
"Than" is مِنْ, and the noun after it ends in -i: أَكْبَرُ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ, bigger than the house.
In a comparison with مِنْ, the form doesn't change for a feminine word or a plural: الْقَرْيَةُ أَصْغَرُ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ, with no ـَة.
English -er doesn't always match: "better" is أَحْسَن or أَفْضَل, and for some describing words Arabic uses أَكْثَر, more, instead.

examples.en: The train is faster than the bus.
This village is smaller than my village.
I ate less than my brother.

why.q_en: Why أَصْغَرُ, with no ـَة, for الْقَرْيَةُ, a feminine word?
why.a_en: In a comparison with مِنْ, this form stays the same for every noun: masculine, feminine or plural. It's one describing word that doesn't match.

selftest.q_en: Which means "bigger than"?
selftest.why_en: The أَـ pattern compares, and مِنْ is "than".

selftest.q_en: Which says "The car is faster than the bus"?
selftest.why_en: أَسْرَعُ stays the same for a feminine word, and سَرِيعَةٌ is just "fast".

selftest.q_en: What does أَقَلّ mean?
selftest.why_en: أَقَلّ comes from قَلِيل, few. "More" is أَكْثَر, and "better" أَحْسَن.

lesson.arabic-quantity-comparison.title_en: Three to ten with a noun: أَرْبَعَةُ أَيَّامٍ, أَرْبَعُ سَاعَاتٍ
lesson.arabic-quantity-comparison.family_en: The number comes first, the noun is plural, and the number takes the opposite gender
steps: From three to ten, the number comes first, and the noun after it is plural and ends in -in: أَرْبَعَةُ أَيَّامٍ, four days. The number's own ending follows its job in the sentence: بَقِيتُ أَرْبَعَةَ أَيَّامٍ, I stayed four days.
Then a surprise: the number takes the opposite gender. With a masculine noun like يَوْم, it has ـَة: أَرْبَعَةُ. With a feminine noun like سَاعَة, it has none: أَرْبَعُ.
Go by the singular: يَوْم is masculine, even though its plural أَيَّام looks different.
One, two and eleven upward follow other rules, so for now learn the phrases you need and check new ones.

examples.en: I stayed in the village for four days.
Our house has five rooms.
Seven students study in our class.

why.q_en: Why أَرْبَعَةُ, with ـَة, for days, when يَوْم is masculine?
why.a_en: From three to ten, the number takes the opposite gender to the singular noun. It's an old rule with no simple reason, so learn it as it is and check the singular each time.

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "four hours"?
selftest.why_en: سَاعَة is feminine, so the number has no ـَة, and the noun is plural.

selftest.q_en: Which is right for "seven days"?
selftest.why_en: يَوْم is masculine, so the number takes ـَة, and the noun is plural.

selftest.q_en: What does خَمْسُ لُغَاتٍ mean?
selftest.why_en: خَمْسُ is five, and لُغَات is the plural of لُغَة.

lesson.arabic-root-pattern.title_en: Roots and patterns: دَرْس, مَدْرَسَة, مُدَرِّس
lesson.arabic-root-pattern.family_en: Three root letters carry an idea; a pattern around them adds a role

table.form_en: a person: from دَرَّسَ, to teach

steps: Most Arabic words are built on a root: usually three letters that carry a general idea. د-ر-س is about studying.

A pattern of vowels and extra letters goes around the root and adds a role. Patterns are named with ف-ع-ل as a stand-in root: مَفْعَلَة often makes a place, so د-ر-س gives مَدْرَسَة, a school; مَفْعَل does the same without ـَة: مَطْعَم, a restaurant.
Not every letter belongs to the root: in مَدْرَسَة, the مَـ and the ـَة come from the pattern.
A shared root isn't a shared meaning. عِلْم, knowledge, and عَالَم, the world, both come from ع-ل-م. Check each word in its sentence or in a dictionary.

examples.en: My brother studies at a nearby school.
The teacher is explaining the lesson.
I studied science at university.

why.q_en: Why doesn't عَالَم, the world, mean something about knowledge, when it shares ع-ل-م with عِلْم?
why.a_en: A root gives you a family, not a definition. Words drift apart over time, and each one has its own meaning. The root helps you remember a word and look it up; the sentence and the dictionary tell you what it means.

selftest.q_en: Which root do دَرْس, مَدْرَسَة and مُدَرِّس share?
selftest.why_en: The مَـ and مُـ come from the patterns. The three letters in all of them are د-ر-س.

selftest.q_en: What does the pattern of مَدْرَسَة often show?
selftest.why_en: مَفْعَلَة often names a place. A person is often فَاعِل, and something done to is مَفْعُول.

selftest.q_en: عِلْم and عَالَم share a root. Do they mean the same?
choices: no: each word has its own meaning
yes: the same root, the same meaning
selftest.answer: no: each word has its own meaning
selftest.why_en: عِلْم is knowledge, and عَالَم the world. A root is a family, not a meaning.

leads_to.en: The doer, the done-to and the action, from one root.
One root, three verbs: عَلِمَ, عَلَّمَ, تَعَلَّمَ.

lesson.arabic-clitic-segmentation.title_en: Taking a word apart: وَ, بِـ, الْـ and ـهُ
lesson.arabic-clitic-segmentation.family_en: Short words joined to the front and endings joined to the back

table.en: for the school, to the school

table.form_en: و is a root letter here
ب is a root letter here

steps: Some short words are written joined to the next word: وَ, and; فَـ, so; بِـ, with or by; لِـ, for or to; كَـ, like; and الْـ, the. Endings like ـهُ join at the back.
To look a word up, peel these off first: وَبَيْتُهُ is وَ, and, then بَيْت, house, then ـهُ, his.
لِـ before الْـ drops the alif: لِـ with الْمَدْرَسَة is written لِلْمَدْرَسَةِ.
Be careful: a و or ب at the start may belong to the word itself. In وَصَلَ, he arrived, and بَحَثَ, he searched, they're root letters.
If two ways of splitting both look possible, let the sentence decide, and check in a dictionary.

examples.en: I went to the market by car.
My brother arrived, so we went together.
This present is for the teacher.

words.en: for the teacher, a woman (لِـ + الْـ + مُعَلِّمَة)

why.q_en: Why does لِلْمَدْرَسَةِ have no alif, when الْمَدْرَسَة has one?
why.a_en: When لِـ comes before الْـ, the alif is dropped in writing, so the two لs sit together: لِلْمَدْرَسَةِ. With بِـ or وَ, the alif stays: بِالْمَدْرَسَةِ.

selftest.q_en: How do you split وَسَيَّارَتُهُ?
selftest.why_en: وَ, and; سَيَّارَة, car, with its ة written ت before the ending; ـهُ, his.

selftest.q_en: In وَصَلَ, he arrived, what is the و?
selftest.why_en: The verb is و-ص-ل, to arrive, so the و is part of it.

selftest.q_en: Which is "for the house"?
selftest.why_en: لِـ before الْـ drops the alif, and the noun ends in -i.

leads_to.en: Finding the word once it's taken apart.

lesson.arabic-dictionary-method.title_en: Using a dictionary: by root or by spelling, and the right sense
lesson.arabic-dictionary-method.family_en: How to find a word, and how to choose the meaning that fits

table.en: a letter; a small grammar word

steps: Some Arabic dictionaries list words by spelling, like an English one. Others list them by root: to find مَدْرَسَة, you look under د-ر-س. The first pages tell you which.
To find the root, take off any joined words and endings, then the pattern's extra letters: الْمَدَارِسُ is الْـ with مَدَارِس, the plural of مَدْرَسَة, root د-ر-س.
An entry gives more than a meaning: the plural of a noun, the present of a verb, and examples. Note the ones you need.
Many words have several senses. Start from the sentence, try a sense, and keep it only if it fits: حَرْف is a letter in a text about spelling, and a small grammar word like فِي in a grammar book.
A translation app can suggest a meaning, but check it the same way.

examples.en: I looked the word up in the dictionary.
The plural of "word" is "words".
There are four letters in this word.

why.q_en: Why look under د-ر-س to find مَدْرَسَة, and not under م?
why.a_en: In a root dictionary, a whole family is listed together under its root letters. The م of مَدْرَسَة belongs to the pattern, not the root, so the word sits under د-ر-س with دَرَسَ and دَرْس.

selftest.q_en: In a root dictionary, where do you find مَدْرَسَة?
selftest.why_en: The مَـ and ـَة come from the pattern; the root is د-ر-س.

selftest.q_en: What is the Arabic grammar word for "plural"?
selftest.why_en: مُفْرَد is "singular", and سِيَاق "context".

selftest.q_en: A dictionary gives three senses. Which do you choose?
choices: the one that fits the sentence
selftest.answer: the one that fits the sentence
selftest.why_en: Try each sense in the sentence, and keep the one whose meaning and grammar fit.

leads_to.en: Recording a word you looked up so you can use it.
Choosing between words that share a spelling.

lesson.arabic-participles-masdar.title_en: The doer, the done-to and the action: قَارِئ, مَقْرُوء, قِرَاءَة
lesson.arabic-participles-masdar.family_en: Three kinds of word made from one verb
steps: From one verb, Arabic makes three useful kinds of word: the doer, the one it's done to, and the action itself.
The doer follows the pattern فَاعِل: قَرَأَ, he read; قَارِئ, a reader. It can name a person, like لَاعِب, a player, or describe one: هُوَ سَاكِنٌ فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ, he lives in Cairo.
The done-to follows مَفْعُول: مَقْرُوء, read; مَعْرُوف, known.
The action is the مَصْدَر, the verbal noun: قِرَاءَة, reading; ذَهَاب, going. Its pattern changes from verb to verb, so learn it with the verb.
These are words, not tenses: قَارِئ can be "a reader" or "reading", depending on the sentence.

examples.en: I love reading stories.
This restaurant is well known in the town.
Getting to work takes me an hour.

why.q_en: Why is the action قِرَاءَة for قَرَأَ, but ذَهَاب for ذَهَبَ?
why.a_en: The doer and done-to patterns are regular for verbs like these, but the verbal noun has many patterns, and you can't tell from the verb which one it uses. Learn it with the verb: قَرَأَ, قِرَاءَة; ذَهَبَ, ذَهَاب.

selftest.q_en: Which word means "a player"?
selftest.why_en: The doer follows فَاعِل. لَعِب is the action, playing.

selftest.q_en: What does مَعْرُوف mean?
selftest.why_en: مَفْعُول is the done-to pattern: known.

selftest.q_en: Which is the action, the مَصْدَر, of دَرَسَ?
selftest.why_en: دِرَاسَة is studying. دَارِس is someone who studies, and مَدْرُوس "studied".

leads_to.en: The doer and the action for longer verbs: مُعَلِّم, تَعْلِيم.

lesson.arabic-vocabulary-records.title_en: Recording a word so you can use it
lesson.arabic-vocabulary-records.family_en: Past and present for a verb, plural for a noun, and a phrase for both

table.en: I drink tea in the morning

steps: A word on its own is easy to recognise and hard to use. Record it in a short phrase you might say: أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ صَبَاحًا.
For a verb, note the past and the present together, شَرِبَ / يَشْرَبُ: the present's middle vowel usually can't be guessed from the past.
For a noun, note the plural, since most plurals can't be guessed either: بَيْت, بُيُوت.
Add how it sounds, and where you met it, so that an old or rare sense doesn't pass for everyday Arabic.
Review by recalling, not rereading: cover the Arabic, say it from the English, then use it in a new sentence.

examples.en: I learn ten words by heart every day.
I remember the word, but I forget its plural.

examples.ar: أَكْتُبُ كُلَّ كَلِمَةٍ جَدِيدَةٍ عَلَى بِطَاقَةٍ.
examples.en: I write each new word on a card.

why.q_en: Why note يَشْرَبُ as well as شَرِبَ?
why.a_en: The present's middle vowel changes from verb to verb: جَلَسَ, يَجْلِسُ; دَخَلَ, يَدْخُلُ; ذَهَبَ, يَذْهَبُ. Three verbs that look alike in the past take three different vowels, so the present is part of learning the verb.

selftest.q_en: What makes a verb record most useful?
choices: the past, the present and a phrase
selftest.answer: the past, the present and a phrase
selftest.why_en: The present can't be guessed from the past, and a phrase shows how to use the verb.

selftest.q_en: What does أَنْسَى mean?
selftest.why_en: "I remember" is أَتَذَكَّرُ, and "I learn by heart" أَحْفَظُ.

selftest.q_en: What is نُطْق?
selftest.why_en: "A card" is بِطَاقَة, and "vocabulary" مُفْرَدَات.

leads_to.en: Learning a word with the words it usually goes with.

lesson.arabic-a2-listening.title_en: Following an account you hear: رِحْلَة, زِيَارَة, عَوْدَة
lesson.arabic-a2-listening.family_en: Events named as nouns, and the words that put them in order
steps: An account often names events as nouns: رِحْلَة, a trip; زِيَارَة, a visit; عَوْدَة, the return. Listen for them to build a timeline.
Then listen for the words that order them: قَبْلَ, بَعْدَ, ثُمَّ and عِنْدَمَا.
Listen closely for لَمْ, لَنْ and لَيْسَ: لَمْ نَزُرْ is "we didn't visit", the opposite of زُرْنَا.
Listen once for the gist, then again for the details you need. One unknown word rarely breaks the whole timeline.

examples.en: The trip was long and enjoyable.

examples.ar: بَعْدَ زِيَارَةِ الْمَتْحَفِ، أَكَلْنَا فِي مَطْعَمٍ.
examples.en: After visiting the museum, we ate in a restaurant.
We didn't visit the castle because of the rain.

why.q_en: Why بَعْدَ زِيَارَةِ الْمَتْحَفِ, with a noun, where English says "after visiting"?
why.a_en: Arabic often names an action as a noun, especially after words like قَبْلَ and بَعْدَ: بَعْدَ زِيَارَةِ الْمَتْحَفِ is literally "after the visit of the museum".

selftest.q_en: What does عَوْدَة mean?
selftest.why_en: رِحْلَة is a trip, and زِيَارَة a visit.

selftest.q_en: You hear لَمْ نَزُرِ الْقَلْعَةَ. Did they visit the castle?
selftest.why_en: لَمْ makes it "didn't": we didn't visit the castle.

selftest.q_en: Which word puts events in order?
selftest.why_en: بَعْدَ is "after". رِحْلَة is a trip, and مُلَاحَظَة a note.

leads_to.en: Listening in several passes, each with its own aim.

lesson.arabic-a2-reading.title_en: Reading a notice: إِعْلَان, دَوْرَة, تَسْجِيل
lesson.arabic-a2-reading.family_en: Its purpose first, then the details you have to act on
steps: Read a notice for its purpose first: what is it about, and what does it want you to do?
Then find the details you have to act on: the day, the time, the place, the price and any deadline.
Keep the details apart: the day a course starts isn't the last day to register.
If something isn't in the notice, such as a price, don't fill it in: write "not stated".

examples.en: The cooking course starts on Monday.
Registration is free until the end of the month.
Contact us for more information.

why.q_en: Why does تَبْدَأُ start with تَـ, when the notice isn't talking to "you"?
why.a_en: دَوْرَة is feminine, so the verb takes the "she" form, which starts with تَـ: تَبْدَأُ الدَّوْرَةُ. A masculine noun takes يَـ: يَبْدَأُ الدَّرْسُ, the lesson starts.

selftest.q_en: A notice says تَبْدَأُ الدَّوْرَةُ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ. What does it tell you?
selftest.why_en: تَبْدَأُ is "starts": the notice says nothing about when the course ends.

selftest.q_en: What is تَسْجِيل?
selftest.why_en: دَوْرَة is a course, and إِعْلَان a notice.

selftest.q_en: The notice gives no price. What do you write?
selftest.why_en: Answer from the notice only, and say when something isn't there.

leads_to.en: Following a whole paragraph: its main point and its links.

lesson.arabic-a2-interaction.title_en: Sorting something out: مُشْكِلَة, حَلّ, هَلْ يُنَاسِبُكَ؟
lesson.arabic-a2-interaction.family_en: Naming a problem, asking what's possible, checking, and agreeing

table.en: I have a problem with my booking
Is it possible to change the room?

table.form_en: does it suit you? (to a man)
does it suit you? (to a woman)

steps: A routine exchange has a goal: ask for what you need, listen to the answer, check it, and agree.
Name the problem simply: عِنْدِي مُشْكِلَةٌ فِي الْحَجْزِ, I have a problem with my booking.
Ask what's possible with هَلْ مِنَ الْمُمْكِنِ, is it possible, and a noun for the action: هَلْ مِنَ الْمُمْكِنِ تَغْيِيرُ الْغُرْفَةِ؟
Ask if something suits them with يُنَاسِبُ, it suits, and "you" as an ending: هَلْ يُنَاسِبُكَ الْمَوْعِدُ؟, does the time suit you?
If you're not sure, check with هَلْ تَعْنِي, do you mean, and say the result again at the end.

examples.ar: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُغَيِّرَ الْحَجْزَ إِلَى يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ.
examples.en: I'd like to change the booking to Friday.

examples.ar: الْغُرْفَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ جِدًّا، هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ غُرْفَةٌ أَكْبَرُ؟
examples.en: The room is very small; have you got a bigger room?

words.en: you have (to a group, or a business)

examples.en: That's possible, and it's a good solution.

why.q_en: Why أَكْبَرُ, with no -un, in غُرْفَةٌ أَكْبَرُ?
why.a_en: Words on the أَفْعَل pattern, like أَكْبَر and أَحْسَن, never take -un, -an or -in, even without الْـ. After a word with -un they end in a plain -u, غُرْفَةٌ أَكْبَرُ, a bigger room; where other words would have -an or -in, they end in -a: فِي غُرْفَةٍ أَكْبَرَ, in a bigger room.

selftest.q_en: How do you ask a woman "Does this suit you?"
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "you" is ـكِ. The verb matches هَذَا, so it stays يُنَاسِبُ.

selftest.q_en: What does حَلّ mean?
selftest.why_en: مُشْكِلَة is a problem, and حَجْز a booking.

selftest.q_en: You're not sure what the receptionist meant. What do you say?
selftest.why_en: هَلْ تَعْنِي, do you mean, checks before you agree.

leads_to.en: Questions that build on what someone has just said.

lesson.arabic-a2-composition.title_en: Writing a short paragraph: time, reason and result
lesson.arabic-a2-composition.family_en: Words that keep the time clear and link a reason to its result
steps: A good short paragraph keeps the time, the people and the reasons clear.
Mark the time when it changes: أَمْسِ with a past verb, غَدًا with سَـ and a present verb.
Give a reason with لِأَنَّ, because. Before an ending it joins up: لِأَنَّنِي, because I; لِأَنَّهُ, because he.
Give the result with لِذَلِكَ, so: كُنْتُ مُتْعَبًا، لِذَلِكَ نِمْتُ مُبَكِّرًا, I was tired, so I went to bed early.
Revise the meaning first: is the time clear, and who is "he"? Then check the grammar.

examples.ar: لَمْ أَخْرُجْ أَمْسِ لِأَنَّنِي كُنْتُ مَرِيضًا.
examples.en: I didn't go out yesterday because I was ill.

examples.ar: كَانَ الطَّقْسُ سَيِّئًا، لِذَلِكَ بَقِينَا فِي الْبَيْتِ.
examples.en: The weather was bad, so we stayed at home.
I'll revise the paragraph tomorrow, then send it.

why.q_en: Why لِأَنَّنِي and لِأَنَّهُ, but لِأَنَّ الطَّقْسَ?
why.a_en: لِأَنَّ is followed either by a noun with the object ending, -a or -an, لِأَنَّ الطَّقْسَ, or by a pronoun ending joined to it: لِأَنَّهُ, because he; لِأَنَّنِي, because I (also written لِأَنِّي).

selftest.q_en: Which word gives a result?
selftest.why_en: لِذَلِكَ is "so". لِأَنَّ gives a reason, and مَثَلًا is "for example".

selftest.q_en: Which says "because I was tired"?
selftest.why_en: لِأَنَّ needs a noun or an ending before the verb. لِذَلِكَ كُنْتُ مُتْعَبًا is "so I was tired".

selftest.q_en: When you revise, what comes first?
selftest.why_en: Fix what hides the time or who's who first, then the grammar.

leads_to.en: More ways to link ideas: but, although, whereas.

lesson.arabic-a2-portfolio.title_en: Describing your level and your next step: مُسْتَوَايَ, أَحْيَانًا
lesson.arabic-a2-portfolio.family_en: Saying what you can do, how often, and what comes next

table.en: My reading is at a good level

steps: To describe your level, say what you can do and with what help: أَفْهَمُ الْأَخْبَارَ الْقَصِيرَةَ بِمُسَاعَدَةِ الْقَامُوسِ, I understand short news with the help of a dictionary.
مُسْتَوَى, level, ends in a long ā written ى. Before "my" it becomes مُسْتَوَايَ.
أَحْيَانًا, sometimes, and دَائِمًا, always, say how often.
Then name one next step: الْخُطْوَةُ التَّالِيَةُ هِيَ الِاسْتِمَاعُ, the next step is listening.

examples.ar: أَحْيَانًا لَا أَفْهَمُ الْأَرْقَامَ فِي الْأَخْبَارِ.
examples.en: Sometimes I don't understand the numbers in the news.

examples.ar: مُسْتَوَايَ فِي الْكِتَابَةِ أَحْسَنُ مِنْ مُسْتَوَايَ فِي الِاسْتِمَاعِ.
examples.en: My writing is at a better level than my listening.
I'll review my progress at the end of the month.

why.q_en: Why مُسْتَوَايَ, with an alif and ـيَ, and not مُسْتَوَى with ـِي?
why.a_en: After a long ā there's nowhere for the -i of ـِي to sit, so "my" becomes ـيَ, said -ya, and the ى is written as a plain alif: مُسْتَوَى, مُسْتَوَايَ.

selftest.q_en: What does أَحْيَانًا mean?
selftest.why_en: "Always" is دَائِمًا.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "my level"?
selftest.why_en: After a long ā, "my" is ـيَ, and the ى becomes an alif.

selftest.q_en: Your listening is weaker than your reading. What's a good next step?
selftest.why_en: Pick the next step from the weaker skill, and keep the rest going.

lesson.arabic-diacritics-taper.title_en: Reading without the vowel marks: the marks, and the clues
lesson.arabic-diacritics-taper.family_en: What each mark is called, and how a sentence settles a word without them

table.form_en: the letters د-ر-س as a verb

steps: Fully vowelled text marks every short vowel: that's the تَشْكِيل. Most Arabic you'll read leaves the marks out.
Each mark has a name: فَتْحَة for a, ضَمَّة for u, كَسْرَة for i, سُكُون for no vowel, and شَدَّة for a doubled letter.
Without marks, one spelling can be several words: the letters د-ر-س can be دَرَسَ, he studied; دَرْس, a lesson; or دَرَّسَ, he taught.
The sentence settles it: after الْـ or فِي it's a noun, and a verb is followed by who did it.
Take the marks away gradually, and keep only the ones you still need to settle a word.

examples.en: I went to the first lesson.
Laylā taught Arabic for two years.
We studied this topic in class.

why.q_en: Without its marks, how can I tell which word د-ر-س is?
why.a_en: From its neighbours. After الْـ or فِي it's the noun, دَرْس. With a doer and something studied after it, it's a verb. If both still fit, keep both in mind and read on: the next words usually decide.

selftest.q_en: Which mark shows a short u?
selftest.why_en: فَتْحَة is a, and كَسْرَة i.

selftest.q_en: What does a شَدَّة show?
selftest.why_en: "No vowel" is سُكُون, and a short a فَتْحَة.

selftest.q_en: In "in the lesson", which reading of د-ر-س fits?
selftest.why_en: After فِي and الْـ, only a noun fits.

lesson.arabic-context-ambiguity.title_en: One spelling, several words: ذَهَب, ذَهَبَ, شَعْر, شِعْر
lesson.arabic-context-ambiguity.family_en: Words that look alike without their marks, and how the sentence chooses
steps: Without marks, different words can share a spelling: ذَهَب, gold, and ذَهَبَ, he went, look the same on the page.
Test each reading: is a verb or a noun needed here? Does it agree with the words around it? Does the meaning make sense?
Neighbours help. A small word like مِنْ or فِي, or الْـ, points to a noun: خَاتَمٌ مِنْ ذَهَبٍ, a gold ring. A doer after it points to a verb.
A dictionary lists the possible senses; the sentence chooses among them.
If the evidence doesn't settle it yet, note each اِحْتِمَال, possibility, and read on.

examples.en: She bought a gold ring.
My grandfather went to the market.
Her hair is very long.

why.q_en: If ذَهَب and ذَهَبَ look the same, why don't readers get lost?
why.a_en: Because a sentence rarely leaves room for both. After مِنْ, only the noun fits: مِنْ ذَهَبٍ, of gold. In ذَهَبَ جَدِّي إِلَى السُّوقِ, "my grandfather's gold" would leave إِلَى السُّوقِ with no verb, so only ذَهَبَ, he went, fits.

selftest.q_en: In شَعْرُهَا طَوِيلٌ, which word is شَعْر?
selftest.why_en: "Her … is long" needs something that can be long: hair. Poetry is شِعْر.

selftest.q_en: Which reading fits مِنْ ذَهَبٍ?
selftest.why_en: After مِنْ comes a noun, ending in -in: gold.

selftest.q_en: The sentence doesn't settle a word yet. What do you do?
choices: note both readings and read on
choose the first meaning you know
selftest.answer: note both readings and read on
selftest.why_en: Keep both possibilities until the text decides.

lesson.arabic-paragraph-mapping.title_en: Following a paragraph: its main point, and the words that link it
lesson.arabic-paragraph-mapping.family_en: Words that add, contrast and sum up, and pronouns that point back
steps: A paragraph has a main point, and the rest supports it, gives examples, or sets something against it. The main point isn't always the first sentence.
Linking words show the relation: بِالْإِضَافَةِ إِلَى ذَلِكَ and كَذَلِكَ add; ثَانِيًا lists; مِنْ نَاحِيَةٍ أُخْرَى sets against; بِاخْتِصَارٍ sums up.
Track each pronoun back to what it means: هِيَ or ـهَا points to a feminine noun or a plural of things, هُوَ or ـهُ to a masculine one, usually the nearest that fits.
Check the match before you move on: a sentence can be understood word by word and still be misread if "it" is pinned to the wrong noun.

examples.en: The town is small, but it's beautiful.

examples.ar: بِالْإِضَافَةِ إِلَى ذَلِكَ، الْمُوَاصَلَاتُ فِيهَا رَخِيصَةٌ.
examples.en: In addition to that, transport there is cheap.
In short, it's a good place to study.

why.q_en: How do I know what ـهَا points to?
why.a_en: Look back for the nearest noun that fits: feminine for ـهَا and هِيَ, masculine for ـهُ and هُوَ, and one that makes sense. In الْمَدِينَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ، وَلَكِنَّهَا جَمِيلَةٌ, the ـهَا is the town.

selftest.q_en: Which phrase sums up?
selftest.why_en: كَذَلِكَ adds, and ثَانِيًا lists a second point.

selftest.q_en: Which phrase brings in the other side?
selftest.why_en: The other two add a point on the same side.

selftest.q_en: In الْمَدِينَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ، وَلَكِنَّهَا جَمِيلَةٌ, what does ـهَا mean?
selftest.why_en: It points back to the nearest feminine noun that fits: الْمَدِينَة.

lesson.arabic-extensive-reading.title_en: Reading at length: the gist, and talking about what you read
lesson.arabic-extensive-reading.family_en: Words for books and reading, and how to read for the main thread
steps: For reading at length, choose something you mostly understand and want to finish: a short رِوَايَة, or an article in a مَجَلَّة.
Read for the main thread, الْفِكْرَةُ الْعَامَّةُ, and stop only for words the story can't do without.
If almost every line needs the dictionary, choose something easier or shorter.
When you finish a section, say its main event in one sentence, then pick a few words worth learning.
أَنْهَى, to finish, takes what you finish straight after it: أَنْهَيْتُ الْكِتَابَ, I finished the book.

examples.ar: أَقْرَأُ عَشْرَ صَفَحَاتٍ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ بِدُونِ قَامُوسٍ.
examples.en: I read ten pages a day without a dictionary.

examples.ar: كَانَتِ الرِّوَايَةُ مُمْتِعَةً، فَأَنْهَيْتُهَا فِي أُسْبُوعٍ.
examples.en: The novel was enjoyable, so I finished it in a week.

examples.ar: فَهِمْتُ الْفِكْرَةَ الْعَامَّةَ مَعَ أَنَّنِي لَمْ أَعْرِفْ كُلَّ الْكَلِمَاتِ.
examples.en: I understood the gist, although I didn't know every word.

why.q_en: Why أَنْهَيْتُ, with يْ, from أَنْهَى?
why.a_en: Verbs ending in ى change it to يْ before endings like ـتُ: أَنْهَى, he finished; أَنْهَيْتُ, I finished. It's the same change as مَشَى, مَشَيْتُ.

selftest.q_en: What is الْفِكْرَةُ الْعَامَّةُ?
selftest.why_en: فِكْرَة is an idea, and عَامّ general.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "I finished the novel"?
selftest.why_en: أَنْهَى takes what you finish straight after it, and its ى becomes يْ before ـتُ.

selftest.q_en: Nearly every line needs the dictionary. What do you do?
choices: choose an easier or shorter text
selftest.answer: choose an easier or shorter text
selftest.why_en: Reading at length works when most of the text is already within reach.

lesson.arabic-collocation-growth.title_en: Words that go together: طَرَحَ سُؤَالًا, حَصَلَ عَلَى
lesson.arabic-collocation-growth.family_en: Verbs and nouns with their usual partners, which a word-for-word translation misses

table.form_en: with بِـ (on its own, قَامَ is "he stood up")

table.en: he took part in the competition

steps: Words have usual partners. "Take a photo" is اِلْتَقَطَ صُورَةً, literally "pick up a picture". أَخَذَ, take, is the everyday word; formal Arabic prefers اِلْتَقَطَ.
So learn a noun with its verb, and a verb with its small word: حَصَلَ عَلَى, to get; شَارَكَ فِي, to take part in.
Look for the pair in a dictionary example or a text, rather than putting it together from English.
Note where a pair belongs: أَلْقَى مُحَاضَرَةً is formal, and fits a talk or a report better than a quick message.

examples.ar: طَرَحَتْ سَلْمَى سُؤَالًا مُهِمًّا فِي الِاجْتِمَاعِ.
examples.en: Salmā asked an important question at the meeting.
We had a lovely time on the beach.
My brother got a new job.

why.q_en: Why does حَصَلَ need عَلَى?
why.a_en: On its own, حَصَلَ means "it happened". With عَلَى it means "to get, to obtain": حَصَلَ عَلَى عَمَلٍ, he got a job. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the verb with it.

selftest.q_en: How do you say "he took part in the race"?
selftest.why_en: شَارَكَ takes فِي for what you take part in.

selftest.q_en: What does أَلْقَى مُحَاضَرَةً mean?
selftest.why_en: أَلْقَى is "to throw" on its own, but with مُحَاضَرَة it's "to give" a lecture.

selftest.q_en: What does حَصَلَ mean without عَلَى?
selftest.why_en: With عَلَى it means "to get".

lesson.arabic-listening-passes.title_en: Listening in passes: سَمِعَ and اِسْتَمَعَ إِلَى
lesson.arabic-listening-passes.family_en: Hearing and listening, and the words for each pass
steps: سَمِعَ is to hear; اِسْتَمَعَ is to listen, on purpose, and it takes إِلَى before what you listen to.
Give each pass its own aim: first the topic, then the details you need, then the language, such as one phrase you missed.
If something is lost, replay that short مَقْطَع, not the whole recording.
Keep apart what you understood بِمُفْرَدِي, on your own, and what you understood with the text in front of you.

examples.en: I listened to the clip three times.

examples.ar: فِي الْمَرَّةِ الثَّانِيَةِ، كَتَبْتُ التَّفَاصِيلَ الْمُهِمَّةَ.
examples.en: The second time, I wrote down the important details.

examples.ar: فَهِمْتُ الْمَوْضُوعَ بِمُفْرَدِي، ثُمَّ قَرَأْتُ النَّصَّ.
examples.en: I understood the topic on my own, then read the text.

why.q_en: Why اِسْتَمَعْتُ إِلَى, but سَمِعْتُ with no small word?
why.a_en: سَمِعَ takes what you hear straight after it: سَمِعْتُ صَوْتًا, I heard a sound. اِسْتَمَعَ, listening on purpose, takes إِلَى: اِسْتَمَعْتُ إِلَى الْأَخْبَارِ. Learn each verb with its partner.

selftest.q_en: Which means "I listened to the news"?
selftest.why_en: اِسْتَمَعَ takes إِلَى.

selftest.q_en: What is a مَقْطَع?
selftest.why_en: Replay a short مَقْطَع rather than the whole recording.

selftest.q_en: What is the first pass for?
selftest.why_en: Details come on the next pass, and the language after that.

lesson.arabic-connected-listening.title_en: Words that run together: هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ
lesson.arabic-connected-listening.family_en: Why a phrase sounds different from its words read one by one

table.form_en: after a word: the alif is silent

steps: In speech, the words of a phrase run together: a space on the page isn't a pause.

The alif at the start of الْـ, of اِسْم and of many commands is هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ, a joining hamza, written with a plain alif. It's said only when you start speaking with it; after another word it's silent, and the words join: فِي الْبَيْتِ.
Before a sun letter, the ل of الْـ is said as that letter: فِي الشَّارِعِ.
Listen to a short phrase at natural speed, look at its words, then say it along with the speaker.
Slowed-down audio helps at first, but aim for natural سُرْعَة, speed.

examples.en: The speaker repeated the sentence twice.

words.en: the speaker (its alif silent after كَرَّرَ)

examples.en: He speaks fast, but clearly.
Listen, then read the text.

words.en: read (its alif silent after ثُمَّ; its last letter takes -i before الْـ)

why.q_en: Why isn't the alif of اِسْمُكَ said in مَا اسْمُكَ؟?
why.a_en: It's a joining hamza: it only helps you start a word from silence. After مَا there's already a vowel to carry you in, so the hamza drops out of speech and the two words join.

selftest.q_en: In فِي الْبَيْتِ, is the alif of الْـ said?
choices: no: after a word it's silent
selftest.answer: no: after a word it's silent
selftest.why_en: It's a joining hamza, said only at the start of speech.

selftest.q_en: What is هَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ?
choices: a hamza said only at the start of speech
a hamza that is always said
a mark for a doubled letter
selftest.answer: a hamza said only at the start of speech
selftest.why_en: The doubling mark is the شَدَّة.

selftest.q_en: What should listening practice aim for in the end?
selftest.why_en: Slow audio is a support on the way.

lesson.arabic-follow-up-questions.title_en: Following up what someone says: مُنْذُ مَتَى؟, مَاذَا تَقْصِدُ؟
lesson.arabic-follow-up-questions.family_en: Questions that build on the answer you've just heard
steps: A follow-up question builds on what the other person has just said, rather than moving on to your next prepared question.
Pick the gap: a reason, لِمَاذَا؟; a time, مُنْذُ مَتَى؟; an example; or what they meant, مَاذَا تَقْصِدُ؟
Keep their words and change "I" to "you": أَعْمَلُ فِي مُسْتَشْفًى, so مُنْذُ مَتَى تَعْمَلُ هُنَاكَ؟
أَيّ, which, goes before a noun ending in -in: أَيُّ كِتَابٍ؟, which book?
If you didn't follow, sort that out first with مَاذَا تَقْصِدُ؟. They may answer with يَعْنِي, "I mean", before explaining.

examples.en: How long have you worked at the hospital?

examples.ar: قُلْتَ إِنَّكَ سَافَرْتَ كَثِيرًا، أَيُّ بَلَدٍ أَعْجَبَكَ أَكْثَرَ؟
examples.en: You said you've travelled a lot: which country did you like most?
What do you mean by that?

why.q_en: Why مُنْذُ مَتَى تَعْمَلُ, a present verb, for "how long have you worked"?
why.a_en: With مُنْذُ, Arabic uses the present for something still going on: مُنْذُ مَتَى تَعْمَلُ هُنَا؟, how long have you been working here? English needs "have been"; Arabic doesn't.

selftest.q_en: Your partner says أَعْمَلُ فِي مَصْنَعٍ. Which question builds on it?
selftest.why_en: It asks about the job they've just mentioned.

selftest.q_en: How do you ask "Which book?"
selftest.why_en: أَيّ goes before a noun ending in -in. أَيْنَ is "where".

selftest.q_en: You didn't follow what they said. What do you ask first?
selftest.why_en: Sort out the meaning before asking anything new.

lesson.arabic-opinion-repair.title_en: Giving an opinion, and putting it another way: فِي رَأْيِي, أَقْصِدُ
lesson.arabic-opinion-repair.family_en: A view, a reason and a limit, and how to rephrase when a word won't come
steps: An opinion has three parts: your view, a reason, and how far it goes. Start the view with فِي رَأْيِي, in my opinion, and the reason with لِأَنَّ.
Limit it when you need to: تَقْرِيبًا, roughly; عَلَى الْأَقَلِّ, at least.
To disagree politely, say what you agree with first, هَذَا صَحِيحٌ, that's right, then your point after لَكِنَّ, but.
When a word won't come, describe it with words you know, then add أَقْصِدُ, I mean, or بِعِبَارَةٍ أُخْرَى, in other words.
A pause to find words isn't a failure. Describing is better than guessing a word you're unsure of.

examples.ar: فِي رَأْيِي، الْمَشْيُ أَفْضَلُ مِنَ السَّيَّارَةِ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ.
examples.en: In my opinion, walking is better than the car in town.

examples.ar: هَذَا صَحِيحٌ، لَكِنَّ الْمَسَافَاتِ طَوِيلَةٌ أَحْيَانًا.
examples.en: That's right, but the distances are sometimes long.

words.en: the distances (-i after لَكِنَّ: ـَات takes -i where others take -a)

examples.en: I mean the nearby neighbourhoods, at least.

why.q_en: Why لَا أُوَافِقُ, with لَا, and not لَمْ أُوَافِقْ?
why.a_en: لَا with a present verb says what's true now: I don't agree. لَمْ أُوَافِقْ is the past: I didn't agree, at some earlier time.

selftest.q_en: Which phrase gives your view?
selftest.why_en: تَقْرِيبًا is "roughly", and بِعِبَارَةٍ أُخْرَى "in other words".

selftest.q_en: What does بِعِبَارَةٍ أُخْرَى bring in?
choices: the same idea in other words
selftest.answer: the same idea in other words
selftest.why_en: عِبَارَة is a phrase or expression: "in another expression".

selftest.q_en: You can't remember a word. What's the best move?
choices: describe it with words you know
selftest.answer: describe it with words you know
selftest.why_en: Then add أَقْصِدُ, I mean, if it helps.

lesson.arabic-speaker-variety.title_en: Standard Arabic, dialects and accents: الْفُصْحَى, الْعَامِّيَّة, لُكْنَة
lesson.arabic-speaker-variety.family_en: The words for the kinds of Arabic you'll hear, and how to treat a difference
steps: الْفُصْحَى, Standard Arabic, is shared across the Arab world in writing, the news and formal speech. Each region also has its everyday speech, الْعَامِّيَّة, in its own لَهْجَة.
A لُكْنَة, an accent, is how someone pronounces: two newsreaders from different countries can both speak الْفُصْحَى, each with their own accent.
So a sound you didn't expect isn't necessarily a mistake: note it and check it before you call it wrong.
Listen to several speakers at different speeds: one familiar voice can hide gaps.

examples.en: The newsreader speaks Standard Arabic with a slight accent.

examples.ar: هَذَا اخْتِلَافٌ فِي النُّطْقِ، وَلَيْسَ خَطَأً.
examples.en: This is a difference in pronunciation, not a mistake.
In formal situations we use Standard Arabic.

why.q_en: Why learn الْفُصْحَى when people speak الْعَامِّيَّة at home?
why.a_en: الْفُصْحَى is the Arabic every country shares in books, the news and formal talk, while everyday speech changes from region to region. It gives you the common core.

selftest.q_en: What is a مُذِيع?
selftest.why_en: A dialect is لَهْجَة.

selftest.q_en: Where is الْفُصْحَى used?
choices: in writing, the news and formal speech
selftest.answer: in writing, the news and formal speech
selftest.why_en: Everyday speech, الْعَامِّيَّة, is what changes from region to region.

selftest.q_en: A speaker pronounces a sound differently from your course. What do you do first?
selftest.why_en: It may be an accent, not an error.

lesson.arabic-paragraph-design.title_en: Building a paragraph: عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْمِثَالِ, أَيْ, هَكَذَا
lesson.arabic-paragraph-design.family_en: One purpose, sentences that add to it, and words that link them
steps: A paragraph serves one purpose: a sentence that states it, sentences that support it, and an ending that rounds it off.
Each sentence should add something: an example, a reason or a result. The same claim again in new words adds nothing.
Bring in an example with عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْمِثَالِ, and check it supports this claim, not a new topic.
Explain a word with أَيْ, that is: الْمُوَاصَلَاتُ الْعَامَّةُ، أَيِ الْحَافِلَاتُ وَالْقِطَارَاتُ, public transport, that is, buses and trains.
Round it off with هَكَذَا, in this way, to show where the paragraph has led.

examples.ar: الدَّرَّاجَةُ أَسْرَعُ مِنَ الْحَافِلَةِ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ.
examples.en: A bike is faster than the bus in town.

examples.ar: عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْمِثَالِ، أَصِلُ إِلَى عَمَلِي فِي عَشْرِ دَقَائِقَ.
examples.en: For example, I get to work in ten minutes.
In this way I save time and money.

why.q_en: What's the difference between عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْمِثَالِ and أَيْ?
why.a_en: عَلَى سَبِيلِ الْمِثَالِ brings in one case among others: for example. أَيْ restates or explains what you've just said: that is. A bike is one example of a way to get around; "public transport, أَيْ buses and trains" names all of it.

selftest.q_en: Which phrase brings in an example?
selftest.why_en: خَاتِمَة names a part of a paragraph, and أَيْ explains: "that is".

selftest.q_en: What is a خَاتِمَة?
selftest.why_en: The opening is a مُقَدِّمَة.

selftest.q_en: Which sentence adds something to "Cycling saves time"?
choices: It takes me ten minutes instead of thirty.
Cycling is a way to save time.
Time can be saved by cycling.
